title: Glyph reference
text:
Each glyph has a name, which links to its definitions and examples. A function glyph also has a name for its monad, which takes one argument, and for its dyad, which takes two. Operators take functions or arrays and derive functions. Notes flag unusual differences from Dyalog APL. Follow each glyph’s link for details and examples. Each function’s page gives its ranks. An argument of higher rank applies the function to each cell of that rank, as Rank does.


The keyboard map shows the Option and Option-Shift bindings, with dead keys outlined in orange.
Hold Alt, which is Option on a Mac, and press the key in the Key column. Keys refer to a US layout. ≤ is Alt-< and ≥ is Alt->, each with Shift held. Where the column shows a second key, press it with or without Alt held. For example, Alt-o c means Alt-o, then c. You can type a shifted second key without Shift. For example, Alt-q ; types ⍠, the same as Alt-q :. An Alt key that takes a second key types its own glyph when Space or an unlisted key follows. For example, Alt-o then Space gives ○. Backspace or Escape cancels the sequence.
Superscripts start with Alt-6. The second key is a digit, - then a digit, t for ᵀ, u for ᵘ, or b for ᵇ. Subscripts start with Alt-5. The second key is a digit, - then a digit, or x, j, e or r for the number suffixes ₓ, ⱼ, ₑ and ᵣ. A glyph with no key, such as +, is on an ordinary ASCII key. The arrows are on hjkl. Alt-[ types nothing, because terminals send it as the start of a control sequence. The identifier characters ∆ and ⍙ are Alt-7, and Alt-Minus then 7.
The names in these tables are the ones you type. In the REPL, a backtick and any of them, then Tab, enters the glyph, as named entry describes. Python exports the function names, with _ in place of - and a trailing _ on Python keywords, as in index_of and and_. It spells operators as properties with their names, as in f.reduce.

Postfix on the token before it, or after a space on the run before it: x² is x*2, f² is f⍣2, f⁻¹ is the inverse of f, mᵀ is ⍉m, and fᵘ is a scalar holding f


₁ ₋₁ subscript
Alt-5

Array positions: v₁ is 1⌷v, v₋₁ is the last major cell, m₁ ₂ is m.[1 2], and v₁←5 assigns to that cell. Function axes: +/₀ is +/⍠0, and +/₁ ₂ is +/⍠[1 2]



Numbers covers numeric notation, such as ₓ, r, j and e.



System names start with •. System functions lists them.




Vectors: a bracket list such as [a b c] is a vector. A strand of literals, such as 1 2 3, needs no brackets. [5] is a one-item vector, the same as ,5. Parentheses group: (5) is 5. A scalar holding 5 is ⊂5. Arrays side by side also form a vector: a b is [a b]. (1 2⋄3) is the vector of rows [[1 2] [3]].
Runs: outside brackets, spaces group an expression into runs, and each run acts as one token. A run that ends in a function is a train: +/÷≢ is the mean, and 2× is 2↣×. An operator takes the token next to it, so after a run that ends in a dyadic operator, the next run is its right operand: in ⌊@ 10× x, it is 10×.
Indexing: brackets are used to write vectors, never to index. Positions and axes count from 0. Negative positions and axes count from the end. Index selects: 0⌷v is the first item of v.
Atoms: numbers, characters and functions are atoms, distinct from scalars, as BQN. Enclosing always adds a layer: ⊂3 ≡ 3 is $f.
Numbers: bare numbers are approximate. ₓ marks an exact integer, and r or ᵣ an exact rational, as in J: 1ₓ÷3ₓ is 1ᵣ3. Predicates, positions, tally and shape are exact. See Mathish mode for comparison and zero-division conventions.
Agreement: pervasive functions, Each and Rank align leading axes. An axis of length 1 expands to match: 2 3⍴⍳6 + 10 20 is [10 11 12⋄23 24 25].
Major cells: ∊ ~ ∪ ∩ compare major cells, N#Y replicates them, N⊂Y and N⊆Y split along the first axis. ⊤ and ⊥ put digits on the last axis, as J.
System names: written •name, as BQN, not ⎕NAME. Most Dyalog system functions and variables are not included.
Axis keys name data. K:Y evaluates its keys. T.a is "a"⊃T. T.(expr) and T⍎Y evaluate with the keys of T as names.
Dfns: BPL has dfns, with no tradfns and no colon control structures such as :If.
Removed forms: Dyalog’s bracket axes f[A], outer product ∘.f, windowed reduce and laminate are not in BPL. Use numeric subscripts or ⍠ for axes, ⊗ for outer products, ↕ for windows, as in +/3↕v, and [x⋄y] for rows. / ⌿ \ ⍀ are only reduce and scan. A left argument to them is a seed, as in BQN: 2+/1 2 3 is 8. Replicate and expand are # and #⁻¹.

title: Glyph reference
text: System names start with •. System functions lists them.

title: Glyph reference
text:
Vectors: a bracket list such as [a b c] is a vector. A strand of literals, such as 1 2 3, needs no brackets. [5] is a one-item vector, the same as ,5. Parentheses group: (5) is 5. A scalar holding 5 is ⊂5. Arrays side by side also form a vector: a b is [a b]. (1 2⋄3) is the vector of rows [[1 2] [3]].
Runs: outside brackets, spaces group an expression into runs, and each run acts as one token. A run that ends in a function is a train: +/÷≢ is the mean, and 2× is 2↣×. An operator takes the token next to it, so after a run that ends in a dyadic operator, the next run is its right operand: in ⌊@ 10× x, it is 10×.
Indexing: brackets are used to write vectors, never to index. Positions and axes count from 0. Negative positions and axes count from the end. Index selects: 0⌷v is the first item of v.
Atoms: numbers, characters and functions are atoms, distinct from scalars, as BQN. Enclosing always adds a layer: ⊂3 ≡ 3 is $f.
Numbers: bare numbers are approximate. ₓ marks an exact integer, and r or ᵣ an exact rational, as in J: 1ₓ÷3ₓ is 1ᵣ3. Predicates, positions, tally and shape are exact. See Mathish mode for comparison and zero-division conventions.
Agreement: pervasive functions, Each and Rank align leading axes. An axis of length 1 expands to match: 2 3⍴⍳6 + 10 20 is [10 11 12⋄23 24 25].
Major cells: ∊ ~ ∪ ∩ compare major cells, N#Y replicates them, N⊂Y and N⊆Y split along the first axis. ⊤ and ⊥ put digits on the last axis, as J.
System names: written •name, as BQN, not ⎕NAME. Most Dyalog system functions and variables are not included.
Axis keys name data. K:Y evaluates its keys. T.a is "a"⊃T. T.(expr) and T⍎Y evaluate with the keys of T as names.
Dfns: BPL has dfns, with no tradfns and no colon control structures such as :If.
Removed forms: Dyalog’s bracket axes f[A], outer product ∘.f, windowed reduce and laminate are not in BPL. Use numeric subscripts or ⍠ for axes, ⊗ for outer products, ↕ for windows, as in +/3↕v, and [x⋄y] for rows. / ⌿ \ ⍀ are only reduce and scan. A left argument to them is a seed, as in BQN: 2+/1 2 3 is 8. Replicate and expand are # and #⁻¹.

title: Style
text:
Style
These forms make BPL easy to read for someone who doesn’t know APL. How a line reads decides between them. Resemblance to APL counts for nothing.
Use spaces to show the top-level structure of an expression. Keep parentheses where they make nested scope easier to see, as in ⍺,(↓key_val,join),⍵. Keep connected tokens in one run. Use ⁝ (Alt-:) where tokens must stay distinct without ending the run: h⁝m, +/⍠i⁝m. Two names that touch merge, as ix does in +/⍠ix. A name followed by a literal stays separate: f1 is f(1). Syntax gives the grouping rules.
A function between two runs takes a space on each side, as in a×b + c. A space on one side only changes the grouping: a×b +c is the strand [a×b ; +c], and a×b+ c applies the train a×b+ to c.
⁝ separates a derived function’s operand from its right argument where a boundary is needed: f⍣3⁝0, 10÷√1++/⍠i⁝m, (+/÷≢)⍤1⁝2 3⍴⍳6. It stops literal stranding without grouping the expression before it. A vector argument can touch the operand in brackets: ≥⍣2[1 2 3]. Add nothing where tokens already stay distinct, as in +/⍤1m or (+/÷≢)⍠d⊼n.
With a left argument as well, ⁝ works the same way, as in Q+.×⍠e⁝r. Parentheses around the derived function also show it between its arguments: 10 20(+⍤1)m. Use whichever reads better. Keep parentheses where a compound operand or nested train needs grouping, as in ⌊@(10×)x.
A space groups the whole run before it, including any prefix. +/÷≢ ⊼y-c+h+.×v applies the mean train to its complete argument. mean_square←+/÷≢ ⊼ separates an atop’s subtrains. f⁝g⁝h x keeps three named functions in one run. +/÷≢⁝v doesn’t group the mean train. For nested parentheses, try removing the inner pair first: (+⌿ N*Ms ÷ ≢N)*÷Ms. Naming a train that a line uses twice can read better: mean⍤1m.
Lowercase j reads most clearly in complex literals, as in 3j4. Uppercase J is an input alias, and only its own tests need it. Archived upstream source keeps its original form. Array notation shows a literal matrix’s rows directly, as in [10 20 30⋄40 50 60], where a reshape hides them. A reshape still suits an example about reshape. A ⋄ between rows reads best with no spaces around it. A ⋄ between statements reads best with a space on each side.
Brackets build a list from names or expressions. A bare literal list, such as 1 2 3, is a shorthand. In brackets, a list of names reads as a list at a glance, as in [a b], even where a b would also work. [n 2]⍴0, [x],y, [a⋄b] and f⍤1 m read more directly than APL’s (n,2)⍴0, (⊂x),y, ⊃[a b] and ⊃f¨↓m. Where no item of a bracket list contains a space, spaces separate the items more lightly than ;: [i j] rather than [i;j].
An operand often reads best touching its operator, with parentheses around a compound operand, as in ⌊@(10×)x and (≢⊢)⌸x. Spacing also makes a run into an operand: after a dyadic operator and a space, the whole next run is the operand, as in ⌊@ 10× x. When both operands are compound, parentheses around each show the grouping: (•ucs 9)@(⍸tabs)⍵. An operand keeps its parentheses when a left argument comes before it, as in tree (⍺⍢)/ next. Report any case where none of these forms reads well.
A train reads more directly than naming an argument twice: +/÷≢ v rather than +/v ÷ ≢v. A tacit form usually reads more directly than a dfn. A dfn reads better where the tacit form would be longer or clearly awkward.
fib10 means fib 10, not an identifier, which would be fib_10. That form reads well where it’s shorter and needs no new parentheses. 32•float∞ converts ∞ to a 32-bit float, as 32 •float ∞ does with spaces it doesn’t need. 32 •float∞ gives the two items 32 64ₓ instead: the runs 32 and •float∞ strand, and •float∞ alone gives ∞’s width. When spaces separate names in a dyadic call, keep both: x f 5 rather than x f5.
⌷ reads clearly for a selection, as in [⍋v]⌷v. Use numeric subscripts for literal positions, as in v₁, m₁ ₂ and v₁←0, and for literal axes, as in +/₁ and +/₂ ₃. Keep ⍠ for named or computed axes and options records. . suits other assignment targets, such as v.[i]←0, record fields, such as T.name, and places where ⌷ would be longer. A target that is a cross product of positions takes ⌷ with a spaced ←, as in [1 3;0 5]⌷a +←10. . pairs its index arrays instead: a.[1 3;0 5] selects only the items at positions 1 0 and 3 5.
Positions and counts are exact, while bare numbers are floats. Arithmetic that mixes the two gives floats. Under dynamic kinds, a write that mixes them leaves the array in mixed storage. ⍳10ₓ and ⍳≢x give exact positions, where ⍳10 gives floats. An array that will hold positions or counts stays exact when it starts from exact numbers, as in n⍴¯1ₓ, with a counter starting at 0ₓ. On positions, ≥i, i+1ₓ and 2ₓ×i stay exact, where i+1 and 2×i give floats. For an exact v, +/÷≢ v gives an exact rational. +/÷1×≢ v gives a float. Where a map’s branches give Booleans and numbers, converting the Boolean gives one type: +b gives exact integers, and 1×b gives floats.

title: Regex
text:
]help •r

•r — Regular expressions
•r pattern compiles a regular expression. It returns a keyed vector of two functions that share the pattern. p.matches text gives a table of the matches, as a record of columns: text, the matched text; position, its position in characters from 0; and groups, the text of each group, which is empty for a group that took no part. template p.replace text replaces each match with template, expanded with the match’s groups.
Natively the pattern uses fancy-regex’s syntax, including lookaround and backreferences. Flags go in the pattern, as in (?i), and templates use $1, ${name} and $$. A search that exceeds the engine’s backtracking limit raises DOMAIN. In the browser the pattern is a JavaScript regular expression, with JavaScript’s syntax, and templates use $1, $<name> and $$. Regular expressions covers each function.
p←•r "([a-z]+)([0-9]+)"
p.matches "ab12 cd3"           ⍝ ["text":["ab12" "cd3"] "position":[0 5]ₓ "groups":("ab" "12"⋄"cd" "3")]
"$2:$1" p.replace "ab12 cd3"   ⍝ "12:ab 3:cd"
Errors: DOMAIN for invalid patterns and non-text arguments; SYNTAX for the wrong valence; LIMIT for oversized results.


Natively, patterns use fancy-regex syntax, including lookaround and backreferences. Exceeding the engine’s backtracking limit raises DOMAIN. In the browser they use JavaScript’s. p.matches gives a table of the matches, as a record of columns. Here p finds runs of digits:

p←•r "[0-9]+"
p.matches "abc123def45"

["text":["123" "45"] "position":[3 9]ₓ "groups":[0⍴⊂"" 0⍴⊂""]]


Matches don’t overlap. Positions count characters, and ≢¨ of the text column gives each match’s length. A text with no match gives a table with no rows:

m←(•r "é|🐈+").matches "aé🐈🐈z"
m.position
≢¨m.text
(•r "é|🐈+").matches "abc"

[1 2]ₓ


[1 2]ₓ


["text":0⍴⊂"" "position":⍬ₓ "groups":0⍴⊂0⍴⊂""]


The groups column holds the captured strings of each match, without the whole match. An unmatched optional capture gives "":

p←•r "([a-z]+)([0-9]+)"
(p.matches "ab12 cd3").groups

("ab" "12"⋄"cd" "3")


template p.replace text replaces each match with template. In a native template, $0 is the whole match and $$ is a literal $. An unknown or unmatched capture expands to "". In the browser, templates use JavaScript’s syntax, where $<word> names a group:

p←•r "(?P<word>[a-z]+)([0-9]+)"
"${word}:$2:$$" p.replace "ab12"

ab:12:$


Natively, inline flags change how a pattern matches. (?i) ignores case. (?m) makes ^ and $ match at each line break. (?s) makes . match line breaks too. Use Each to search several strings:

p←•r "(?i)cat"
{≢(p.matches ⍵).text}¨"Cat cat" "dog"

[2 0]ₓ


Empty matches occur at character boundaries:

p←•r ""
(p.matches "é🐈").position
'-' p.replace "é🐈"

[0 1 2]ₓ


-é-🐈-


lib/regex.bpl supplies pattern f regex_replace text. It applies f to each matched string and keeps the text between matches:

[regex_replace:]←•load "../lib/regex.bpl"
"[0-9]+" {⍕⊽•json⍵}regex_replace "a12 b3"

a24ₓ b6ₓ

text:
Choose a demo to run it. The Code tab holds its BPL, which you can edit and run again with ▶ Run, or Ctrl-Enter (Cmd-Enter on a Mac). Reset brings back the demo’s own code and runs it. Each run starts a new session. The interpreter runs in your browser, as in the playground.

title: •deflate — Compression
text:
•deflate — Compression
•deflate bytes decompresses gzip data and returns the bytes. •deflate⁻¹ data compresses data with gzip. It compresses text as UTF-8, and numbers as bytes from 0 to 255, as •nput writes them. Both directions take a format name on the left: "gzip", "zlib" or "deflate" (raw DEFLATE).
•ucs •deflate •deflate⁻¹ "hello"          ⍝ "hello"
"zlib" •deflate "zlib" •deflate⁻¹ 1 2 3   ⍝ [1 2 3]ₓ
Errors: DOMAIN for an unknown format, byte values outside 0 to 255, or data that doesn’t decompress.

title: •uuid — UUIDs
text:
•uuid — UUIDs
•uuid v returns a new UUID of version v as text. Version 4 is random. Version 7 UUIDs begin with their creation time and sort in creation order. Version 0 is the nil UUID, with every digit zero. Versions 1 and 6 also hold the time, with a random node in place of a MAC address.
[ns name] •uuid 5 derives a UUID from a name with SHA-1, and [ns name] •uuid 3 with MD5. ns is "dns", "url", "oid", "x500" or a UUID. The same namespace and name always give the same UUID. bytes •uuid 8 makes a UUID from 16 bytes, and sets its version and variant.
"dns" "python.org" •uuid 5   ⍝ "886313e1-3b8a-5372-9b90-0c9aee199e5d"
Errors: DOMAIN for any other version, or a left argument that doesn’t fit the version.

title: •metadata — File metadata
text:
•metadata — File metadata
•metadata paths gives a table with a row for each path, as a record of columns. The columns follow Rust’s std::fs::Metadata:



Column
Gives




path, name
The path as given, and its last part


kind
"file", "dir", "symlink" or "other", or "none" for a path that doesn’t exist


target
For a symbolic link, the path it points to, as Rust’s std::fs::read_link gives it. Empty for any other entry


len
The size in bytes


modified, accessed, created
Moments, in seconds since the Unix epoch, as •date reads them. NaN where the system records none


readonly
Whether the permissions forbid writing


hidden
Whether the name starts with .


readable, writable, executable
Whether this process may read, write or execute the entry


uid, mode, owner
On Unix only: the owner’s numeric ID, the mode bits and the owner’s name



A symbolic link’s kind is "symlink". Its other columns describe the entry it points to.
Errors: DOMAIN when a path isn’t text.

title: •csv — CSV
text:
•csv — CSV
•csv text parses CSV into a vector of columns. Headers become keys. Numeric columns become numbers. Missing numeric cells become the fill option’s value, NaN by default. A fill takes its column’s type wherever it keeps its value in that type: ["fill":0] reads 0ₓ at each missing cell of an integer column. A fill that doesn’t keep its value, such as NaN or 0.5 in an integer column, makes the column floats. Missing text cells become "".
Under static kinds, every integer column reads at the int width whatever its values, as every new integer does. A value that doesn’t fit is a DOMAIN error that names the column.
The types option sets the type of columns, each from a value of that type. A number, such as 0ₓ₈, 0ₚ or $f, makes a numeric column of its type. Each of the column’s values, and the fill at its missing cells, must keep its value in that type, or the read is a DOMAIN error. A float type rounds to its width. Text, such as "", reads a column as written: 02134 stays "02134". A record sets the columns that it names. A vector sets every column in order. It needs one value for each column, as a file with no header does:
•prefs ["kinds":"static"]
t←"id,price,flag,zip",(•ucs 10),"3000000000,1.5,1,02134",(•ucs 10),"7,2.25,0,10001"
T←["types":["id":0ₓ₈ "price":0ₚ "flag":$f "zip":""]] •csv t
T.id                       ⍝ [3000000000 7]ₓ₈
T.flag                     ⍝ $t $f
(•storage T.price).kind    ⍝ "float64"
T.zip                      ⍝ "02134" "10001"
•prefs ["kinds":"dynamic"]
["header":$f "types":["" 0ₓ]] •csv "a,12",(•ucs 10),"b,7"   ⍝ [["a" "b"] [12 7]ₓ]
•csv⁻¹ T writes CSV text for a vector of columns. Keys supply the header. Column lengths must agree. NaN writes as an empty cell, and so does the exact value given as fill.
Both directions take options on the left: header, separator, quotechar, doublequote, escapechar, decimal, thousands, trim and fill. Reading also takes missing and types, and writing takes forcequotes and lineending. "forcequotes":2 quotes every field. CSV describes the options.
Errors: DOMAIN for invalid options, duplicate headers, and cells that CSV can’t hold: rationals that aren’t whole, complex numbers, functions or nested cells, and for a value that doesn’t keep itself in its column’s type; LENGTH for unequal record widths or columns, or a types vector of the wrong length.

title: •svg — SVG pictures
text:
•svg — SVG pictures
X •svg children returns an svg element with attributes X. It adds xmlns for the SVG namespace and viewBox="0 0 100 100". Attributes in X replace these. Notebooks display it as a picture. XML and SVG covers element trees.

title: •r — Regular expressions
text:
•r — Regular expressions
•r pattern compiles a regular expression. It returns a keyed vector of two functions that share the pattern. p.matches text gives a table of the matches, as a record of columns: text, the matched text; position, its position in characters from 0; and groups, the text of each group, which is empty for a group that took no part. template p.replace text replaces each match with template, expanded with the match’s groups.
Natively the pattern uses fancy-regex’s syntax, including lookaround and backreferences. Flags go in the pattern, as in (?i), and templates use $1, ${name} and $$. A search that exceeds the engine’s backtracking limit raises DOMAIN. In the browser the pattern is a JavaScript regular expression, with JavaScript’s syntax, and templates use $1, $<name> and $$. Regular expressions covers each function.
p←•r "([a-z]+)([0-9]+)"
p.matches "ab12 cd3"           ⍝ ["text":["ab12" "cd3"] "position":[0 5]ₓ "groups":("ab" "12"⋄"cd" "3")]
"$2:$1" p.replace "ab12 cd3"   ⍝ "12:ab 3:cd"
Errors: DOMAIN for invalid patterns and non-text arguments; SYNTAX for the wrong valence; LIMIT for oversized results.

title: •nl — Name list
text:
•nl — Name list
prefix •nl classes lists the visible user names in classes that begin with prefix, as a sorted vector of strings. •nl classes lists them all. Introspection has examples.
Errors: DOMAIN for unsupported classes; RANK for a class matrix.

title: •decompose — Matrix decompositions
text:
•decompose — Matrix decompositions
kind •decompose m factors the matrix m and returns the factors as a record. kind names the decomposition, as text or as the kind of a record of options:








kind
Fields
Factors




"svd"
u, s, v
m is u×⍤1s +.× +⍉v, with the singular values s in descending order


"qr"
q, r
m is q+.×r, with orthonormal columns in q, and r upper triangular


"eigen"
values, vectors
each column of vectors is an eigenvector of m, for the eigenvalue at the same position in values


"cholesky"
l
m is l+.×+⍉l, with l lower triangular


"lu"
l, u, p
[p]⌷m is l+.×u, with l lower triangular with 1 on its diagonal, u upper triangular, and p the rows’ positions



The SVD and the QR decomposition are thin, unless option complete asks for the complete QR. For an r-by-c matrix, u and q have r⌊c columns. The factors are floats, apart from "lu"’s positions p. A real matrix gives real factors, apart from complex eigenvalues and their eigenvectors. A Hermitian matrix, one equal to its conjugate transpose, has real eigenvalues in ascending order and orthonormal eigenvectors. Each eigenvector of a real matrix has unit length. ⌹ solves linear systems.
("svd" •decompose [1 2⋄3 4⋄5 6]).s     ⍝ 9.525518091565104 0.5143005806586441
("eigen" •decompose [2 1⋄1 2]).values  ⍝ [1 3]
Where option vectors is false, "svd" and "eigen" give only s or values, in less time. It’s true by default. Where option complete is true, "qr" gives a square q, and an r with as many rows as m. It’s false by default.
(["kind":"svd" "vectors":$f]•decompose [1 2⋄3 4⋄5 6]).s   ⍝ 9.525518091565104 0.5143005806586441
⍴(["kind":"qr" "complete":$t]•decompose [1 2⋄3 4⋄5 6]).q  ⍝ [3 3]ₓ
Option rank, a positive whole number, makes "svd" give only the first rank singular values, with their vectors unless vectors is false. A randomized method computes them, in far less time than the full SVD of a large matrix takes. The result is an approximation. The faster the singular values beyond the rankth decay, the smaller its error. For a rank within 10 of the matrix’s smaller side, the result is the full SVD’s first rank columns.
(["kind":"svd" "rank":1]•decompose [1 2⋄3 4⋄5 6]).s   ⍝ [9.525518091565104]
⍴(["kind":"svd" "rank":1]•decompose [1 2⋄3 4⋄5 6]).v  ⍝ [2 1]ₓ
The determinant is -.×m. The "lu" factors give its sign, and the logarithm of its magnitude, which can’t overflow:
f←"lu" •decompose [1 2⋄3 4]
f.p                       ⍝ [1 0]ₓ
d←0 0⍉f.u
-.×f.p=⊗⍳≢f.p × ×/×d     ⍝ ¯1ₓ
+/⍟|d                     ⍝ 0.6931471805599453
kind •decompose⁻¹ factors multiplies a record of factors back into the matrix, as the table shows. For "eigen", the matrix is vectors×⍤1values +.× ⌹vectors, and for "lu" it’s [⍋p]⌷l+.×u. Eigenvectors that aren’t independent, such as those of the defective matrix [1 1⋄0 1], can’t determine the matrix.
f←"cholesky" •decompose [4 2⋄2 3]
"cholesky" •decompose⁻¹ f   ⍝ [4 2⋄2 3]
Errors: RANK for an argument that isn’t a matrix, or a factor of the wrong rank; LENGTH for "eigen", "cholesky" or "lu" of a matrix that isn’t square, or factors whose sizes don’t agree; DOMAIN for an unknown decomposition or option, a vectors of false for a kind other than "svd" and "eigen", a complete of true for a kind other than "qr", a rank that isn’t a positive whole number or that’s given for a kind other than "svd", an empty or nonnumeric matrix, "cholesky" of a matrix that isn’t Hermitian positive definite, a missing factor, eigenvectors that aren’t independent, or a p that doesn’t hold each position once.

title: •load — Load
text:
•load — Load
•load path runs the BPL file at path as a module, with names of its own. It returns a record of the module’s public names: the names its top level assigns that don’t start with _. The file adds no names to the caller, and shows nothing except explicit output. Each call runs the file again.
Take names with a pattern, as in [a: b:]←•load path, or keep the record and read names with a dot, as in m←•load path and then m.a.
A path that starts with ./ or ../ is relative to the file holding the code. Other relative paths are relative to the working directory. •nget and •nput follow the same rule.
Errors: IO for a file that can’t be read; DOMAIN for a file that loads itself, directly or through other files.

title: •nget — Read a file
text:
•nget — Read a file
•nget path reads a UTF-8 text file. •nget "-" reads the rest of standard input. A path that starts with ./ or ../ is relative to the file holding the code, as for •load.
X •nget path takes options on the left: binary (1 reads a vector of byte values) and encoding ("UTF-8"). Files covers bytes and options.
Errors: IO for missing files, invalid UTF-8, other file errors, and standard input that fails or that the frontend doesn’t provide; DOMAIN for invalid options.

title: •json — JSON
text:
•json — JSON
•json text reads JSON5, which includes all JSON. JSON5 adds comments, trailing commas, single-quoted strings, unquoted keys, hexadecimal numbers, Infinity and NaN. Objects become keyed vectors. Arrays become vectors. Strings become character vectors. Integers of up to 128 bits stay exact. true and false become $t and $f.
•json⁻¹ Y writes JSON text. Keyed axes become objects. Unkeyed axes become arrays. Character vectors become strings. Keyed entries that hold functions are left out. NaN writes as null.
["fill":v] •json text reads null as v. The fill takes its array’s type wherever it keeps its value in that type: ["fill":0] •json "[1,null,3]" gives [1 0 3]ₓ, and ["fill":0] •json "[true,null]" gives $t $f. A fill that doesn’t keep its value, such as the default NaN beside integers, makes the array floats. ["fill":v] •json⁻¹ Y writes v as null. JSON covers the conversions.
Under static kinds, an array of integers reads at the int width, and a value that doesn’t fit is a DOMAIN error. ["types":R] •json text gives the arrays that fields hold a type: R maps a field’s name to a number of that type, as •csv’s types option does, and every array that a field of that name holds takes it:
•prefs ["kinds":"static"]
(["types":["id":0ₓ₈]] •json "{""id"":[3000000000,7],""n"":[1,2]}").id    ⍝ [3000000000 7]ₓ₈
•prefs ["kinds":"dynamic"]
Errors: DOMAIN for malformed JSON, with its line and column, and for values that JSON can’t hold: an infinity that isn’t fill, out-of-range floats, rationals that aren’t whole, complex numbers and other functions. Also DOMAIN for a value that doesn’t keep itself in its array’s type, and for a types entry that names no field holding an array.

title: •readdir — List a directory
text:
•readdir — List a directory
•readdir dir gives the table of •metadata with a row for each entry of dir, sorted by path. Each row’s path is dir joined with the entry’s path within dir. A glob on the left keeps the entries whose path within dir matches it, as in "*.csv" •readdir "data". As in a shell, * stays within one directory and ** crosses them. Options on the left: glob, and recurse (1 also lists the entries of subdirectories).
Errors: IO for a directory that can’t be read; DOMAIN for an invalid glob or option.

title: •memory — Memory
text:
•memory — Memory
•memory x gives a record of what this thread holds, and of what x keeps alive. •memory 0 is the usual spelling for the counts alone.

records counts the live record nodes: the linear calls that reverse mode records while ∂ runs. Each ∂ frees its record when it returns, so the count is 0 between programs.
pending counts the live pending arrays, whose items wait for their first read.
bytes counts the bytes that x keeps alive: its items, the base of a view, the arrays that a pending array reads, the parts of a value that ∂ is differentiating, and the nodes of a record. An allocation that x reaches twice counts once.

records and pending count the nodes that this thread made, even when another thread holds one. •memory reads no items, so it never forces a pending array, and it accepts values that ∂ is differentiating.
{+/⍵×⍵}∂ 1 2 3     ⍝ 2 4 6
•memory 0          ⍝ ["records":0ₓ "pending":0ₓ "bytes":0ₓ]
A reshape is a view, which keeps all of its base’s items alive:
v←⍳1000ₓ
m←2 500⍴v
(•memory m).bytes  ⍝ 2000ₓ
•explain reports what happened while an expression ran.

Run these examples in the playground, the interactive prompt (REPL), or a BPL notebook. Work through them in order, trying a few changes of your own.
A glyph is a written symbol, such as +. To get help on one at the REPL, type ]help +. The glyph reference has the full definitions.
BPL works with values such as numbers and arrays. Start by entering a few numbers.

text: An operator takes one or two values, called operands, and produces a derived function. For example, / turns its operand + into the summing function +/. We’ll use operators to choose axes, combine functions and repeat calculations.

title: System functions
text:
A system function is a built-in function whose name starts with •, as in •ucs or •json. Type • with Alt-y. Names are case-insensitive. Many system functions take their options as a left argument. A function named for a format reads that format, and its inverse writes it: •json reads JSON, and •json⁻¹ writes it. Each name below links to its page. ]help •name shows the same page. Built-in values have names that start with $, as Constants and $ names describes.
A function that takes one string, such as •json or •element, applies to each string of an array of strings, and to each row of a character matrix, as ⍎ does. A function that takes one number, such as •uuid, applies to each number of an array. The results form an array of the argument’s shape. Results from a character matrix’s rows combine as Rank’s results do. An empty argument gives an empty array of the function’s usual result, such as an empty list of strings from •src. A left argument applies whole to each item. •c, •date, •path and •metadata have their own rules for arrays, which their pages give.
In Python, the workspace object bpl has each system function under its name without •. Options become keyword arguments, as in bpl.json('{"a": null}', fill=0). .undo gives the inverse, as in bpl.json.undo(Y) for •json⁻¹. Python covers the calling conventions.

title: Language principles
text:
BasedPL (BPL) keeps APL’s glyphs and its right-to-left evaluation. It changes the notation where APL’s rules make code harder to read or to write. Most of the changes follow from one decision, to write lists in brackets. BasedPL stands for Based-array Programming Language, after the array model it takes from BQN.
Many of the notation choices answer problems that Marshall Lochbaum, BQN’s author, lists in his notes on BQN’s problems and on its first five years. Syntax and Evaluation state the rules without the reasons. BPL, APL and BQN side by side shows the choices on real code.

title: Language principles
text:
Lists are written in brackets
In APL, arrays written side by side form a list. 1 2 3, a b c and (x+1) y are all vectors. This is called stranding. It’s short, but it gives a space a different job in different places. Between arrays, a space separates the items of a list. Between functions it means nothing: +/÷≢ and + / ÷ ≢ are the same train. Between an operator and an array, it can do either.
That last case causes real trouble. An operator takes the single value to its right as its operand, after stranding has already joined that value to its neighbours. In APL, the operand in f⍤1 M is 1 M. You have to write f⍤1⊢M, where ⊢ is there only to break the strand. BQN’s documentation gives the example a +˝∘×⎉1‿∞ b, a matrix product. No rule decides well which of 1, ∞ and b should strand together. BQN marks its strands with ‿ instead.
In BPL, lists are written in brackets, [a b c], as in Python and JavaScript. Lochbaum notes that new BQN programmers “are always expecting [] to be the list notation, and it’d let you copy-paste JSON too”. A list of literals can still leave its brackets out, as in 1 2 3 and "no" "yes". Inside brackets, names and literals mix freely:

x←5
[1 x 3]

1 5 3


Outside brackets, arrays side by side form a list too, whatever the names hold. +/x 3 is a two-item list whether x is a vector or a matrix. Each run, a stretch of code with no spaces in it, is one item of the list. In a b+1 the items are a and b+1. A bracket list is one run like any other:

a←1 ⋄ b←2
a b+1
[1 2] 3

1 3


[[1 2] 3]


A bracket list is a vector, however many items it has. [1] is a one-item vector, not a number:

⍴[1]

[1]ₓ


Parentheses only group, as they do in maths. (1 2) is the same value as 1 2. To make a scalar, enclose with ⊂, as in BQN. ⊂[1 2] is a scalar holding a vector, with no axes:

⍴⊂[1 2]

⍬ₓ


A function after ⊂ makes a train instead, as in ⊂+. The scalar holding + is written +ᵘ.
Array notation extends brackets to higher ranks, as Dyalog’s does. Rows separated by ⋄, or written on separate lines, become major cells:

[1 2
 3 4]

1 2
3 4


The result has one more axis than each row. Rows that are numbers have no axes, and give a vector. Rows that are one-item vectors give a column:

[1⋄2]
[[1]⋄[2]]

1 2


1
2


[a⋄b] is the Mix of [a b] when a and b have the same shape.
In parentheses, rows form a new level of nesting instead of a new axis. Each row is one item of a vector, read as if written in brackets. The rows can have different lengths:

≢¨(4⋄4 5⋄4 5 6)

[1 2 3]ₓ


A row holding one string is still a vector of one item. ("ab"⋄"cd") holds two one-item vectors, while ["ab" "cd"] is the vector of two strings:

≢¨("ab"⋄"cd")
≢¨["ab" "cd"]

[1 1]ₓ


[2 2]ₓ


Items in brackets can be functions. [+/ ÷ ≢] holds three functions. Without the spaces, [+/÷≢] holds one, the mean:

≢[+/ ÷ ≢]
≢[+/÷≢]

3ₓ


1ₓ


Writing a function expression in brackets is one way to make it a value. In BQN this takes ⊑⟨Expr⟩ or a name, a problem Lochbaum lists as “Converting a function expression to a subject is tricky”. The other way is fᵘ, a scalar holding the function f.
Items in a list are evaluated left to right, as statements are. BQN chose the same order for its lists and strands. Here each item prints as it’s evaluated, before the list itself displays:

[⎕←1 ⎕←2]

1
2


1 2

title: Language principles
text:
Spaces group
Outside brackets, literals separated by spaces form a strand, as in 1 2 3. Every other space separates runs. A run is a sequence of tokens with no spaces between them. Each run is evaluated first, as if it were in parentheses:

c←3 ⋄ d←4
a+b×c+d
a+b × c+d

15


21


A space can separate a derived function from its argument: +/⍤1 m applies +/⍤1 to m. A run ending in a dyadic operator takes the next run as its operand, as if no space came between them. A literal argument after a space still joins the operand’s strand, as in f⍤1 2 3, whose operand is 1 2 3. The separator ⁝ (Alt-:) keeps tokens apart without ending the run. It separates names that would merge and literals that would strand. All three of these sum each row:

m←2 3⍴⍳6ₓ
+/⍤1 m
+/⍤ 1 m
+/⍤1⁝2 3⍴⍳6ₓ

[3 12]ₓ


[3 12]ₓ


[3 12]ₓ


A space after an operator also lets a longer function be its operand without parentheses. ⌊@ 10× rounds down to one decimal place, with 10× as the operand of @:

⌊@ 10× 1.24 3.57

1.2 3.5


Lochbaum describes the problem that runs solve, under “Modifiers look looser than trains without spaces”. In BQN’s ⋆∘-×˜, the - looks closer to ⋆, but it binds to ×˜. Writing ⋆∘- ×˜ shows the structure. He calls it “unfortunate that this is something the writer must do rather than something the notation encourages”. In BPL the space is part of the notation.
Under “Long trains are hard for humans to parse”, he notes that readers lose track of a train’s structure after four to eight parts. Runs let spaces show that structure. ⌊ +/÷≢ is the floor of the mean:

⌊ +/÷≢ 1 2 4

2ₓ


Code that is fully spaced, or not spaced at all, groups as in APL. Only mixed spacing changes the grouping. A reader used to APL reads 1+2 × 3 as 7, but here it’s 9:

1+2 × 3

9


A tool that normalises spaces would change a program’s meaning. Other languages give spaces meaning too. K reads a -1 differently from a - 1. Nim tried an experimental mode in which the spaces around an operator changed its precedence, and removed it in version 0.20.

title: Language principles
section: A run that ends in a function is a train
text:
A run that ends in a function is a train
A run that ends in a function has no argument yet. It’s a function, built as an APL train with one addition. A subject before a function binds the one part after it, as 2 does in 2×. Here 32+1.8× converts Celsius to Fahrenheit:

f←32+1.8×
f100

212


The rest follows APL’s train rules. A bound part forms an atop, which gives the same result as Dyalog’s fork with a subject on the left, as in 0.5×⊢+÷. Binding covers the common case of fixing a left argument, without ↣. K has the same idea, called projection, in which 2* is a function.
+/÷≢ nums and +/÷≢nums differ only in the space before nums. The first applies the train +/÷≢, the mean, to nums. The second is one run ending in a subject, the expression +/(÷(≢nums)):

nums←1 2 3 6
+/÷≢ nums
+/÷≢nums

3


1ᵣ4


If both spellings meant the same, the space would mean nothing. In everyday arithmetic the two readings agree. When the functions have arrays between them, as in 32+1.8×, the train gives the same result as the expression. The readings differ only where a fork gets a function as its left part, as in 0.5×⊢+÷. APL has the same split, with nothing in the source to mark it. Removing the argument from APL’s 0.5×⊢+÷⍵ turns it into a fork with a different meaning. In BPL the space shows which reading you get.

title: Language principles
text:
Selection is a function
Index, ⌷, selects. I⌷Y takes one item of I for each leading axis of Y. In K, v 1 selects, because K treats a list as a function of its positions. In BPL v 1 is a strand, because subjects and functions stay apart. One literal position can be written more briefly as a subscript, as in v₁:

v←10 20 30 40
1⌷v
v₁

20


20


Selecting with a number drops that axis from the result. Selecting with an array of positions puts the array’s shape in place of the axis. [⊂1]⌷v gives a scalar holding the item, [[1]]⌷v a one-item vector, and [[2 0]]⌷v two items:

[⊂1]⌷v
[[1]]⌷v
[[2 0]]⌷v

⊂20


[20]


30 10


Dyalog has the same rule, but its v[1] looks like a one-item list and gives a scalar. A one-item result needs v[,1].
Because Index takes its positions on the left, its right argument can be any expression. With sales keyed by city and month, "NY"⌷+/sales selects New York’s total with no parentheses:

sales←["NY" "LA";"jan" "feb"]:[1 2⋄3 4]
sales
"NY"⌷+/sales

   jan feb
NY   1   2
LA   3   4


3

title: Language principles
text:
Counting from 0
Positions and axes count from 0, as in BQN, J, K, Python and NumPy. Negative positions count from the end.

A Boolean is a valid position, as in c⌷"no" "yes". With 1-origin, the position would be 1+c.
Positions run from ¯n to n-1 with no gap. With 1-origin, position 0 is an error that sits between the first item and the last.
n|i wraps a position round a vector of length n. ⌊i÷n and n|i give the row and column of a flat position.
The Python API returns positions from functions such as grade and where. Those positions must agree with Python and NumPy, which count from 0.

Here the comparison is the position:

3>2 ⌷ "no" "yes"

yes


To count from 1, use Range: ↦10 is the numbers 1 to 10. Code from APL books and libraries assumes 1-origin and needs converting.
Two rules follow J and BQN where 0-origin left a choice. A negative length counts down, as J’s i._3 does:

⍳¯3

2 1 0


Interval Index counts the boundaries at or below each value, as BQN’s does. Below the first boundary the count is 0. A position there would be ¯1, which selects the last item:

1 3 5⍸0 3 9

[0 2 3]ₓ


A computed position follows the same rule. In w.[i-1], the position for i=0 is ¯1. It reads the last item, as w[i-1] does in Python. Code that wants another edge says so, as n|i-1 wraps and 0⌈(n-1)⌊i-1 clamps:

w←10 20 30 40 ⋄ i←⍳4ₓ
w.[i-1ₓ]
w.[0⌈3⌊i-1ₓ]

40 10 20 30


10 10 20 30

title: Language principles
text:
Based arrays
BPL uses BQN’s based array model. Numbers, characters and functions are atoms. An array is a rectangular collection of values. Atoms are not arrays. Enclosing always adds a layer: ⊂3 is a rank-0 array holding 3, a different value from 3. Enclosing it again gives depth 2:

⊂3 ≡ 3
≡⊂⊂3

$f


2ₓ


In APL’s nested array model, enclosing 3 gives 3 again. Under the based model, every value has one representation, whether you pass it to a function, return it, or store it in an array. Functions are atoms too. [+/ ÷ ≢] is a list of three of them. Lochbaum’s page on the model gives the longer argument.

title: Language principles
section: Under static kinds, number types don’t depend on values
text:
Under static kinds, number types don’t depend on values
Under static kinds, a number’s type comes from how the program writes or computes it, never from its value. A type that changed with the data would let a program that works on one input behave differently on another. Static kinds are the setting for performance work, such as training neural networks. Performance shows what they speed up. Dynamic kinds, the default, are for convenient interactive analysis. Their integers are exact and never wrap, and their float comparisons are tolerant. Some of their results take their type from their values: √¯4 is complex where √4 is a float. Under either setting, BPL doesn’t make a float exact because it happens to be whole: 2.0 is a float, and so is 2.0+1. A program that wants exact integers asks for them with ₓ.

title: Language principles
text:
Functions act on major cells
BPL follows BQN’s leading-axis model. A function that works on a whole array acts on its major cells, the cells along its first axis. The last-axis glyphs ⌽ / \ , are the leading-axis functions applied at rank 1. Their first-axis twins ⊖ ⌿ ⍀ ⍪ are the leading-axis functions themselves. Every function therefore treats a matrix by the same rule.
Search follows that rule. ⍳ ∊ ~ ∪ ∩ compare the major cells of the searched argument, which for a matrix are its rows. Here ~ removes every row that is 1 2, leaving a one-row matrix:

rows←[1 2
      3 4
      1 2]
rows~[1 2⋄5 6]
⍴rows~[1 2⋄5 6]

3 4


[1 2]ₓ


The other argument’s cells have the same rank. A unit has no major cells to search. To remove the spaces from a string, give ~ the string " ". Giving it the character ' ', a unit, is a RANK error:

"a b c"~" "

abc


Partition splits along the first axis too, into blocks of major cells. Here new blocks start at rows 0 and 2:

1 0 1⊂rows

[[1 2⋄3 4] [1 2⋄]]


⊂⍤1 partitions each row instead, and ⊂₁ splits a matrix into blocks of columns.
Encode and Decode put digits on the last axis, as J’s #: and #. do. Encode turns each number of a vector into a row of digits. Decode turns the rows back into numbers:

d←2 2 2⊤5 6
d
2⊥d

1 0 1
1 1 0


5 6


At rank 0, the function gets each atom as itself and each array item enclosed in a scalar. BQN’s ⎉0 encloses atoms as well. The depth of each 0-cell shows the difference:

≡⍤0 [1 [2 3]]

[0 2]ₓ


As a result, ⊢⍤0 returns its argument unchanged, even when the argument is nested. A function under ⍤0 sees numbers as literals and selection give them. Each, ¨, gives the function the items themselves.

title: Language principles
text:
Names pair axes
Without names, arithmetic pairs axes by position, from the leading axis, as Agreement describes. Where axes have names, they pair by name instead. The same names pair, wherever their axes sit. A name meets an unnamed axis by position, and the result keeps the name. Different names never pair. In arithmetic they build a grid, as an outer product does.
Pairing by position can pair the wrong axes. Here r has a row for each item of a batch and a column for each output. bias has a value for each output. Leading axes pair bias with the rows instead. Because the two lengths agree, no error shows the mistake:

r←2 2⍴⍳4ₓ ⋄ bias←[10 20]ₓ
r+bias

With names on both, bias pairs with the outputs:

r←["b":2 "o":2]⍴⍳4ₓ ⋄ bias←["o":2]⍴[10 20]ₓ
r+bias

Selection follows the same rule, so a formula written with named indices reads as index notation, as einsum’s letters do. •index gives an index a fresh hidden name, which can’t collide with the names on a caller’s data. An index used twice pairs with itself, so m.[i i] is a diagonal:

m←[1 2 3⋄4 5 6⋄7 8 9] ⋄ i←•index 3
m.[i i]

No feature requires names. A function written for plain data also runs on named data. Where it gives other values there, the names express alignment. Named axes gives the full rules.

title: Language principles
text:
Results rather than errors
A form that has a reasonable meaning gives a result, not an error. BPL accepts a result that would be a bug in some programs, with no error, when the result buys useful behaviour or speed. Negative positions are one case, as “Counting from 0” shows. ⌈ beside NaN is another. It gives NaN or the other argument, whichever the processor’s fastest instruction gives. The answer can differ between platforms.

title: Numbers
text:
A bare number such as 0.5 is approximate: a float of the default width: 64 bits under dynamic kinds and 32 under static kinds, unless •prefs sets a width. A number marked with ₓ, such as 3ₓ, is an ordinary integer, exact under the default dynamic kinds. 1r3 is an exact rational. A byte-count suffix such as ₓ₄ selects a fixed-width integer. Comparisons give Booleans, written $t and $f.





Written
Value




3, 0.5, 1E¯3, 1ₑ¯3
Approximate numbers. e, E or ₑ writes an exponent


¯2
A negative number. ¯ is part of the number, and - is a function


3ₓ
An exact integer


3ₓ₁, 3ₓ₂, 3ₓ₄, 3ₓ₈
A fixed-width integer occupying 1, 2, 4 or 8 bytes


1r3, 1ᵣ3
An exact rational


2j3, 2J3, 2ⱼ3
A complex number, 2 + 3i, with approximate parts


∞, ¯∞
Infinities


$n
NaN


$t, $f
True and false


1.5ₕ, 1.5ₛ, 1.5ₚ
A 16-bit, 32-bit or 64-bit float, whatever the default width


2j3ₛ, 2j3ₚ
A complex number with 32-bit or 64-bit parts. 2j3ₕ has 32-bit parts too


⍬, ⍬ₓ, ⍬ₕ, ⍬ₛ, ⍬ₚ
The approximate, the exact, and the 16-bit, 32-bit and 64-bit empty vector


[…]ₓ, (…)ₓ
A list, or rows, in which every number is exact


[…]ₕ, […]ₛ, […]ₚ
A list, or rows, in which every real number is a 16-bit, 32-bit or 64-bit float, and every complex number has parts of that width, or 32-bit parts after ₕ


xⱼy, xₑy, xᵣy
Between two items, such as names: x+y×0ⱼ1, x×10*y and the exact quotient of xₓ by yₓ, as one term



A plain e, j or r starts a name unless the rest of a number follows it, as in 1e5, 1r3 and 2j3. Results display with the subscript forms, as in 1ᵣ3, 2ⱼ3 and 1ₑ20. A subscript form that the rest of a number doesn’t follow, or one between two other items such as names, joins the items on each side into one term, as a literal is one, with the value the table gives. A literal on the left gives what the all-literal form gives: with n←3, 2ₑn is 2ₑ3.
1j2+3j4              ⍝ 4j6
1E¯3                 ⍝ 0.001
¯2+5                 ⍝ 3
2J3≡2j3              ⍝ $t
1ᵣ3≡1r3              ⍝ $t
edges←3 ⋄ 2edges     ⍝ 2 3
x←2 ⋄ n←3 ⋄ xⱼn      ⍝ 2j3
2ₑn                  ⍝ 2000



Exact arithmetic grows as needed. Mixing exact and approximate numbers gives an approximate result. Examples on these pages write ₓ for exact input.
1÷3                  ⍝ 0.3333333333333333
1ₓ÷3ₓ                ⍝ 1r3
1r3+1r6              ⍝ 1r2
1r2+0.5              ⍝ 1
9223372036854775807ₓ+1ₓ ⍝ 9223372036854775808ₓ
A function keeps exact integers exact only if every finite result it gives for them is rational. Arithmetic, !, and * with an integer exponent keep them exact. √, ⍟, π, ○ and monadic * give approximate results, whole ones included. An exact function gives the float ∞ at a pole, such as ÷0ₓ:
2ₓ*¯2ₓ               ⍝ 1r4
!20ₓ                 ⍝ 2432902008176640000ₓ
√4ₓ                  ⍝ 2
÷0ₓ                  ⍝ ∞
Predicates, positions, tally, shape, and monadic ⌊, ⌈ and × return exact integers. A float beyond the i64 range floors to an exact big integer:
⌊2.5 ¯2.5            ⍝ [2 ¯3]ₓ
⌊2*70                ⍝ 1180591620717411303424ₓ
Iota and random integer generation keep an exact argument exact. An argument that must be a whole number, such as an index or a count, accepts a float within 1E¯14 of one, whatever the mathish setting:
⍳10×0.1×3          ⍝ 0 1 2



Numbers that an operation puts in one array share a kind. A float among exact integers makes them all floats, and a complex number makes every number complex:
⍳3ₓ , 0.5            ⍝ 0 1 2 0.5
⍳2ₓ , 1j2            ⍝ 0 1 1j2
1ₓ,0.5 ÷ 2ₓ          ⍝ 0.5 0.25
Each number written in a literal list or in brackets keeps its own exactness, even beside numbers of the other kind. Floats written beside complex numbers become complex. Their values don’t change:
1ₓ 0.5÷2ₓ            ⍝ 1r2 0.25
[1ₓ 0.5]÷2ₓ          ⍝ 1r2 0.25
Under dynamic kinds, a write keeps each number’s exactness too. A float assigned among exact integers, or an exact integer among floats, leaves the array mixed, however the array was made. A Boolean written among other numbers, or a number written among Booleans, leaves it mixed in the same way. Under static kinds, the whole array takes the compact type that holds both its items and the items written, as catenating them would: a float written among bytes makes the array floats. Only items that no compact type holds, such as characters among numbers, leave it mixed. Mixed storage is slower. To keep an array compact, write values of its own kind, as the style guide shows. •explain lists each write that left an array mixed, in its mixed record. To give an existing array one kind, convert it: ⌊ makes exact integers, ×1 makes floats, and +0ₓ compacts items that already share a kind:
r←["a":2ₓ "b":3ₓ]
r.b←2.5
r                    ⍝ ["a":2ₓ "b":2.5]
m←3⍴$f
m.[[1]]←1
m                    ⍝ $f 1 $f
Around literals, […]ₓ and (…)ₓ make every number exact, at any depth. Each number must be whole. After a list or group that holds anything else, as after a name, ₓ floors to exact integers, as Superscripts and subscripts describes. A vector of exact integers displays as […]ₓ, and rows of them as (…)ₓ. ⍕ writes them the same way:
[1 0 1]ₓ≡1ₓ 0ₓ 1ₓ    ⍝ $t
[[1 2] 3]ₓ≡[1ₓ 2ₓ;3ₓ]   ⍝ $t
(0 1⋄2 3)ₓ≡[[0 1]ₓ [2 3]ₓ]  ⍝ $t
1↑⍬ₓ                 ⍝ [0]ₓ
⍕1ₓ ¯2ₓ              ⍝ "[1 ¯2]ₓ"



An ordinary integer literal such as 1ₓ, or an unmarked float or complex literal, is weak. Python int, float and complex arguments are weak too. Arithmetic on weak values gives weak ordinary results. A strong operand makes the ordinary result strong.
An explicit float-width literal or a fixed-width integer is strong. So is a number read by •json or •csv. Constructing an array makes its items strong. Selecting an item preserves that strength.



(•storage x).kind names an array’s storage kind. Ordinary integers report integer regardless of their byte width. Fixed-width integers report their type, such as uint8 for ₓ₁. Mixed storage keeps each item’s own kind. A literal list of exact and approximate numbers uses it:
x←1ₓ 0.5 2ₓ
(•storage x).kind      ⍝ "mixed"
Rationals and exact integers beyond 64 bits have no compact storage. An array that holds one uses mixed storage, as does an array that holds numbers together with characters, nested arrays or functions. A JSON object or a Python dict reads as a literal of its fields does, so its storage is mixed only where the fields need it.
Selecting from, catenating or assigning into mixed storage keeps each item’s kind. A selection or catenation whose items one compact storage holds uses it, as the same items written in brackets do: 1↓'a' 1ₓ 2ₓ is held as integers. An assignment into mixed storage leaves it mixed. Arithmetic builds fresh storage from its results, and each result keeps its own kind. Every result of 1×x is approximate, which makes it a float array. 1ₓ×x keeps the exact results exact:
x←1ₓ 0.5 2ₓ
(•storage 1×x).kind    ⍝ "float64"
(•storage 1ₓ×x).kind   ⍝ "mixed"
Display depends on an array’s items, not on how they’re stored. Boxed display marks an array whose items differ in kind with +, and one whose items are all exact integers with ₓ, whichever storage holds them.
Ordinary integer storage keeps each item in 1, 2, 4 or 8 bytes. One byte holds 0 to 255. Literals, reductions and positions take the fewest bytes that hold every item. Pervasive arithmetic keeps its arguments’ size, and moves to the next size up when a result doesn’t fit. An exact result beyond 8 bytes becomes a big integer in mixed storage. The size never changes an ordinary result, and •storage doesn’t show it. Imported typed integer buffers use the fixed-width rules below.



The suffix gives a number of bytes. ₓ₁ selects unsigned u8; ₓ₂, ₓ₄ and ₓ₈ select signed i16, i32 and i64. The width stays with a value through selection, rebuilding and arithmetic. Integer results wrap at their selected width rather than growing. The int preference does not override an explicit fixed width.
255ₓ₁+1ₓ            ⍝ 0ₓ₁
255ₓ₁+↑[1]ₓ         ⍝ 256ₓ
32767ₓ₂+1ₓ          ⍝ ¯32768ₓ₂
200ₓ₁∧199ₓ₁         ⍝ 120ₓ₁
[200 100]ₓ₁<300ₓ     ⍝ $t $t
Two fixed integers compute at the wider type. In arithmetic, catenation, union and writes, a weak ordinary integer takes the fixed type if it fits, and raises otherwise. A strong ordinary integer makes the result ordinary, under the current kinds setting. Booleans take the fixed type too. Floats follow their existing promotion rules. True division gives 32-bit floats for u8 and i16, and 64-bit floats for i32 and i64, no wider than the float preference. Under static kinds, where the default is 32 bits, i32 and i64 divide to 32-bit floats too. Comparisons give Booleans without requiring a weak argument to fit the fixed type.
Functions that rearrange or select items keep the fixed type, as sort and ↑ do. So do functions whose results can’t exceed a fixed argument: ⍳, ↦, roll, deal, ⊤ and monadic ⨸. Functions built from +, - and × compute at the fixed type and wrap, as +/ does. These are ⊥, polynomial evaluation with ⌻, !, the determinant -.× and the permanent +.×. A result of ∧, ∨ or ! that doesn’t fit the fixed type wraps, as a sum does. Positions, counts and values that can exceed the argument’s range are ordinary integers, such as the results of ⍸, ⍋, ≢ and ⍭. A function with no kernel at the fixed width gives what static kinds give at that width: ○ on u8 gives complex numbers with 32-bit parts. ⌹ and polar ∧ give fixed integers floats of the width that their division gives. A roll of fixed integers gives fixed integers, and a bound of 0, which rolls a float, is a DOMAIN error.
⍳3ₓ₁            ⍝ [0 1 2]ₓ₁
2ₓ⊥(9⍴1ₓ)ₓ₁     ⍝ 255ₓ₁
[0 1]ₓ₁,9ₓ      ⍝ [0 1 9]ₓ₁
⍸[0 1 1]ₓ₁      ⍝ [1 2]ₓ
⍳256ₓ₁ fails, because the literal 256ₓ₁ doesn’t fit u8. ⍳ₓ₁ 256ₓ gives 0 to 255 as u8.
Fixed integer literals must fit their type. After a value, a sized suffix converts to that type. Integer narrowing wraps. Float and rational conversion floors, as ⌊ does, then clamps to the target range. NaN converts to zero; infinities convert to the range’s bounds. Typed empty vectors use the same suffix, as in ⍬ₓ₁.
Plain ₓ makes a fixed integer ordinary. The result is strong. Under dynamic kinds it shares the array’s data without copying, and its arithmetic is then exact. Under static kinds it converts the array to the int width, the type of every ordinary integer there.
Reductions retain the promoted fixed type. A suffix on a function converts its result after computation. To widen the accumulator itself, use a typed reduction seed. Superscripts and subscripts covers the suffix syntax.



Floats come in three widths: 64, 32 and 16 bits. •storage gives their kind as "float64", "float32" and "float16". •float converts an array to any of them. A 64-bit float holds about 16 significant digits, a 32-bit float about 7 and a 16-bit float about 3. They take 8, 4 and 2 bytes. The largest finite 16-bit float is 65504.
Bare numbers are floats of the default width: 64 bits under dynamic kinds and 32 under static kinds, until •prefs ["float":16], ["float":32] or ["float":64] sets one width for both. Code parsed after the change reads its numbers at the new width. In a REPL or a notebook, that is the next input. Leading •prefs calls on a literal record run before the rest of their code is parsed. A script, a notebook cell, a module or ⍎ text that starts with •prefs ["float":32] therefore reads its own numbers at 32 bits. Numbers that •csv, •json and •vfi read also take the default width. So do random numbers, the numbers that •image reads, and floats that a function gives from exact arguments, such as √2ₓ. Times from •time and •date are always 64-bit, because a 32-bit float holds seconds since 1970 only to within about two minutes. ₕ marks a 16-bit float, ₛ a 32-bit float and ₚ a 64-bit float, whatever the default. Display marks floats of the other widths, once after an array’s notation. •literal⁻¹ marks every float. Its text therefore reads back the same at any default.
⊢.kind¨•storage¨[1.5ₕ 1.5ₛ [1.5 2.5]ₚ ⍬ₛ]       ⍝ "float16" "float32" "float64" "float32"
[1.5 2.5]ₛ                          ⍝ [1.5 2.5]ₛ
•literal⁻¹ 0.5                     ⍝ "0.5ₚ"
An operation on floats computes at their width. An exact operand rounds to the width that the operation computes at. Floats of two widths compute at the wider, except that a weak number takes the width of the floats beside it. Writes, catenation and arrays built from items follow the same rule: v,2.5, v₀←2.5 and [v₀ 2.5] keep a 32-bit v’s width. No operation widens floats on its own.
v←32 •float 1.5 2.5
⊢.kind¨•storage¨[v×2ₓ v×v *v v×2 v×2ₚ v×v₀ v,2.5 [v₀ 2.5]]       ⍝ "float32" "float32" "float32" "float32" "float64" "float32" "float32" "float32"
•float v                     ⍝ 32ₓ
32•float1.5 × 16777217ₓ    ⍝ 25165824
Complex numbers have 64-bit or 32-bit parts. •storage gives their kind as "complex128" and "complex64", after their whole size. They follow the rules for floats. A complex number takes the width of the floats it comes from, and a 16-bit float that becomes complex takes 32-bit parts. A complex number beside a float computes at the wider of their widths. A complex result with no imaginary part is a float of its parts’ width. ₛ, ₚ and ₕ mark the width of the parts, and display marks parts that aren’t of the default width:
⊢.kind¨•storage¨[[2j3]ₛ;[2j3]ₕ;√[¯4]ₛ;[2j3]ₛ×1.5]       ⍝ "complex64" "complex64" "complex64" "complex64"
√¯4ₛ                                       ⍝ 0j2ₛ
Each operation on 16-bit floats computes in 32 bits and rounds its result to 16 bits. For + - × ÷ and √, that gives the result of 16-bit arithmetic. Folds, scans and inner products keep their running totals in 32 bits. Only their results round to 16 bits. A 16-bit total of these numbers would stop growing at 256:
+/ 16•float4096⍴0.1   ⍝ 409.5ₕ
An exact operand converts straight to 32 bits, not to 16. A count larger than 65,504, the largest 16-bit float, still divides a 16-bit sum:
h←16 •float 100000⍴1 0
+/÷≢ h                   ⍝ 0.49975586ₕ
Power ⍣∞ stops at two results within relative tolerance 1E¯14 of each other, or within 4 units in the last place for 16-bit and 32-bit results. See Mathish mode for comparison and division rules.



Pervasive functions on floats, such as ÷, *, ⍟ and ○, give results within 4 units in the last place of the correctly rounded result. Rustymath’s Accuracy page lists the exceptions.
Some results are exact. Powers, roots and cube roots whose exact result is a float give it exactly. A logarithm to base 2 or 10 is exact at a power of its base. ○y, and * of a complex number whose imaginary part is y, give an exact direction where y is the float nearest a whole number of quarter turns, up to 256 of them. ○π0.5 is then exactly 0j1. With Mathish mode off, as in these examples, = is exact:
•prefs ["mathish":$f]
7*5 = 16807          ⍝ $t
3√27 = 3             ⍝ $t
10⍟1000 = 3          ⍝ $t
○π0.5 = 0j1          ⍝ $t
•prefs ["mathish":$t]
Last bits aren’t reproducible. A calculation can give results that differ in their last bits on another platform or build, in another run, with another number of threads, at another array size, or by another route, such as one fused loop in place of separate calls. +/ adds in an order that depends on the array’s size, the number of threads and the route. The result at a NaN argument, which NaN it is and the sign of a zero result can differ in the same ways, as rustymath’s Accuracy page describes. ⌈ and ⌊, for example, can give either argument where one is NaN or both are zeros of opposite signs. Compare floats from different routes within a tolerance, as Mathish mode’s = does.
A form that BPL doesn’t recognise as a fast combination, such as one that names a constant, can give different digits, beyond the last bits where the combination is more accurate. ⍟1+x computes through log1p and keeps the digits of a tiny x. one←1 ⋄ ⍟one+x computes ⍟ of 1+x, which loses them.



Mathish mode is on by default. For Mathish types, floating comparisons use relative tolerance 1E¯14, measured against the larger magnitude, and 0÷0 and 1⍟1 give zero. Disable it with •prefs ["mathish":$f] for exact floating comparisons and NaN at floating zero divided by zero.
The calculation’s kind and kinds setting decide whether these conventions apply. Explicit 64-bit float suffixes and imported buffers follow the same rule as literals. Static calculations and fixed-integer operations never use Mathish conventions, even when their floating computation uses 64 bits. The narrower floats keep exact comparisons and raw division. Acceptance of integer and Boolean arguments and convergence stopping rules are independent of Mathish mode.



Floats include ∞, ¯∞, NaN and ¯0 besides finite numbers. An undefined result is NaN rather than an error, except for Mathish mode’s zero divided by zero. 1÷0 is ∞, and ⍟0 is ¯∞. NaN is written $n:
[0÷0 ∞-∞]            ⍝ 0 $n
[1÷0 ⍟0]             ⍝ ∞ ¯∞
Under =, NaN equals nothing, as in IEEE. ≡, search, grade and Key treat NaN as one value, and grade puts it after every other number:
$n=$n                ⍝ $f
$n≡$n                ⍝ $t
Complex arithmetic follows the num_complex crate. A complex number can have infinite or NaN parts.
An infinity or NaN is a float. Joining one to exact integers makes them floats, as any float does:
⍳3ₓ , ∞              ⍝ 0 1 2 ∞
(•storage ⍳3ₓ , ∞).kind   ⍝ "float64"
CSV and JSON imports give NaN for a missing number. An integer column with gaps then becomes floats. A column that also holds an integer too large for a float to hold exactly keeps each item’s kind, in mixed storage.
⌊ and ⌈ return an exact argument unchanged beside an infinity:
3ₓ⌊∞                 ⍝ 3ₓ
The ⌈ and ⌊ pages give their results beside NaN. Arithmetic with an infinity gives floats.



Some functions choose a result’s kind from their arguments’ values. √¯4 is complex because the argument is negative, 1j0 is a float because its imaginary part is zero, and an exact integer that overflows grows. Under •prefs ["kinds":"static"], a result’s kind follows from the function and its arguments’ kinds alone. A fused computation needs that, because it decides each result’s kind before it runs. Real arguments give real results, with NaN outside a function’s domain, and complex results stay complex. ⌊, ⌈ and monadic × of floats give floats, and integer ÷ gives floats. With ₓ after them they give integers, as Rust’s as converts a float: NaN gives 0, and a value past the int width’s range gives its largest or smallest integer:
•prefs ["kinds":"static"]
√¯4 9                ⍝ $n 3
0j1×0j1              ⍝ ¯1ⱼ0
⌊2.5 ∞               ⍝ 2 ∞
7ₓ÷2ₓ                ⍝ 3.5
⌊ₓ2.5 ¯2.5           ⍝ [2 ¯3]ₓ
7ₓ÷ₓ2ₓ               ⍝ 3ₓ
⌊ₓ $n ∞              ⍝ [0 2147483647]ₓ
0÷0                  ⍝ $n
0.7=0.1+0.6          ⍝ $f
•prefs ["kinds":"dynamic"]
Ordinary integers compute at the width that the int pref sets, 32 bits by default, or at a wider integer’s width, and wrap where a result doesn’t fit. An ordinary integer is a fixed integer of the int width. Display marks a fixed integer of that width with plain ₓ. Their storage takes that width too, whatever their values. Code that wants narrow storage writes a fixed type, such as ₓ₁. New floats take 32 bits, unless the float pref sets a width. Fixed integers retain their explicit type. An integer beside a float takes the float’s width. A weak number beside floats takes their width, as under dynamic kinds. Exact fractions stay exact. ⌹ and polar ∧ give integers floats of the width that ÷ gives them. A roll of integers gives integers, and a bound of 0, which rolls a float, is a DOMAIN error. Floating comparisons are exact. An ordinary integer literal that doesn’t fit the int width is a LIMIT error. •csv and •json read integers at the int width too, and their types option gives a column another type:
•prefs ["kinds":"static"]
2147483647ₓ+1ₓ             ⍝ ¯2147483648ₓ
[1 2]ₓ₄+1ₓ                 ⍝ [2 3]ₓ
(•memory ⍳100ₓ).bytes      ⍝ 400ₓ
(•memory ⍳100ₓ₁).bytes     ⍝ 100ₓ
(•storage (32•float1 2)×2ₚ).kind    ⍝ "float64"
(•storage (32•float1 2)×2ₓ).kind    ⍝ "float32"
•prefs ["kinds":"dynamic"]
Performance explains why static kinds are the setting for performance work. Code for static kinds gives each integer the width that its values need and gives •csv and •json a types record for their columns. Code written for dynamic kinds can give other results. Dynamic kinds give this total of positions exactly. Static kinds wrap it at the 32-bit range, unless a 64-bit seed widens the sum:
+/⍳100000ₓ                 ⍝ 4999950000ₓ
•prefs ["kinds":"static"]
+/⍳100000ₓ                 ⍝ 704982704ₓ
0ₓ₈+/⍳100000ₓ              ⍝ 4999950000ₓ₈
•prefs ["kinds":"dynamic"]
Under static kinds, a write whose items have another kind converts the whole array to the compact type that holds both kinds, where one exists. The array’s type then doesn’t depend on which items the write selects. Under dynamic kinds, each written item keeps its own kind in mixed storage:
v←[1 2 3]ₓ₁ ⋄ v.[[1]]←0.5 ⋄ (•storage v).kind    ⍝ "mixed"
•prefs ["kinds":"static"]
v←[1 2 3]ₓ₁ ⋄ v.[[1]]←0.5 ⋄ (•storage v).kind    ⍝ "float32"
•prefs ["kinds":"dynamic"]



Comparisons give Booleans. So does every function whose result is a truth value, such as ~, ∊, ⍷ and ≡. $t is true and $f is false:
x←3 1 4 1 5
x>2                  ⍝ $t $f $t $f $t
Wherever a number is expected, $t is 1 and $f is 0. +/ counts the true items, # keeps the items a Boolean mask marks, and a Boolean used as an index selects position 0 or 1:
x←3 1 4 1 5
+/x>2                ⍝ 3ₓ
x>2 # x              ⍝ 3 4 5
4>2 ⌷ "no" "yes"     ⍝ "yes"
A float used as a Boolean follows the integer-acceptance rule for 0 or 1.
Arithmetic on Booleans gives integers. ∧, ∨, ⊽, ⊼, ⌊ and ⌈ on two Booleans give a Boolean:
$t+$t                ⍝ 2ₓ
$t∧$f                ⍝ $f
Boolean storage takes one byte for each item. Boxed display marks it with $:
(•storage $t $f).kind   ⍝ "bool"

text:
