title: Composing functions
text:
A run that ends in a function is a train. A train of two functions is an atop: f⁝g Y is f(g Y). A train of three functions is a fork: f⁝g⁝h Y is (f Y)g(h Y). With a left argument, X(f g)Y is f(X g Y) and X(f g h)Y is (X f Y)g(X h Y). Trains gives the rules for longer trains.
mean←+/÷≢ ⋄ mean 2 4 9       ⍝ 5
1 2 (⊣+⊢) 3 4                ⍝ 4 6
In a train, a subject becomes the left argument of the function after it. 32+1.8× converts Celsius to Fahrenheit by multiplying by 1.8, then adding 32.
fahrenheit←32+1.8× ⋄ fahrenheit 100     ⍝ 212
A space keeps a train apart from its argument. +/÷≢ v applies the train to v. Without the space, the one run +/÷≢v reads as +/÷(≢v):
v←2 4 9 ⋄ +/÷≢ v             ⍝ 5
v←2 4 9 ⋄ +/÷≢v              ⍝ 1ᵣ3

title: Composing functions
text:
In a train, ⊢ stands for the right argument and ⊣ for the left. A fork with ⊢ reads well where the argument appears once. ⊢÷+/ divides each item by the sum:
⊢÷+/ 1 2 5                 ⍝ 0.125 0.25 0.625
2 (⊢-⊣) 5                    ⍝ 3
Where a formula uses its argument more than once, each ⊢ makes the reader track the argument again. A function that removes the repeats reads better. Newton’s step towards √2 adds half of x to the reciprocal of x. ⊽⁻¹, the inverse of double, halves:
n←⊽⁻¹+÷ ⋄ n 1.5              ⍝ 1.416666667
0.5×⊢+2÷⊢ gives the same results, but its two ⊢s hide the formula. Where no clear tacit form exists, a dfn names the argument, as in {0.5×⍵+2÷⍵}.

title: Composing functions
text:
Atop, f∘g, applies g and then f. X f∘g Y is f(X g Y). ⌊∘÷ divides, then rounds down:
7 ⌊∘÷ 2                      ⍝ 3ₓ
Over, f⍥g, applies g to each argument before f. X f⍥g Y is (g X)f(g Y). =⍥≢ tests whether two lists have the same length:
"abc" =⍥≢ "xyz"              ⍝ $t

title: Composing functions
text:
Before, A↣f, binds A as the left argument of f. In a train, a subject binds the same way without the glyph: 2× is 2↣×. After, f↢A, binds A as the right argument. ,↢1 appends 1 and -↢10 subtracts 10:
,↢1⁝2 3                     ⍝ 2 3 1
-↢10⁝3                      ⍝ ¯7
With two function operands, ↣ and ↢ form monadic hooks. f↣g Y is (f Y)g Y and f↢g Y is Y f(g Y). Two-function trains in BPL are atops. (3<)↣# Y is (3<Y)#Y. It keeps the items of Y that are greater than 3:
(3<)↣# 2 7 1 8               ⍝ 7 8

title: Composing functions
text:
Self, f⍨Y, is Y f Y. Commute, X f⍨Y, is Y f X:
,⍨"ab"                       ⍝ "abab"
2-⍨10                        ⍝ 8
For a power, a superscript reads more directly than Self: x² rather than ×⍨x.
x←3 ⋄ x²                     ⍝ 9

title: Composing functions
text:
f⁻¹ is the inverse of f, as Superscripts describes. BPL infers the inverses of most compositions. fahrenheit⁻¹ converts back to Celsius:
fahrenheit←32+1.8× ⋄ fahrenheit⁻¹ 212   ⍝ 100
A superscript straight after a number applies to the number. To invert a function that ends in a number, put the function in parentheses:
(+↢3)⁻¹ 10                   ⍝ 7
Without the parentheses, +↢3⁻¹ 10 reads 3⁻¹ as a third. The third strands with 10 into the bound operand. No argument remains. The result is the function +↢[0.3333333333 10].

title: Process interfaces
text:
Run bpl --worker. Send one JSON request per line. Each request gets one flushed JSON reply, in order. Names persist between requests.
{"code":"v←⍳10"}
{"id":2,"code":"+/v"}
The second reply is:
{"id":2,"result":{"value":45.0,"output":[{"kind":"display","data":{"text/plain":"45"}}],"error":null}}
id is optional. A reply carries its request’s id, or null for a request without one. Give an id to any request you might interrupt: {"interrupt":2} cancels request 2 and gets no reply of its own. Keep one evaluation outstanding.
Build each request with a JSON encoder, such as Python’s json.dumps or JavaScript’s JSON.stringify, and end it with a newline. The encoder escapes newlines in the source. Stdout contains only replies. EOF ends the session.
Malformed JSON, an invalid field or an invalid encoded array gives an error of kind REQUEST in that request’s result. The session continues.


code evaluates BPL source. timeout_ms sets a deadline. "echo":false suppresses implicit display, but not explicit output.
{"id":1,"code":"+/⍳10","timeout_ms":2000,"echo":false}
bindings maps names to encoded values. call applies a function to one or two encoded args, without generating BPL source.
{"id":2,"call":"+","args":[2,3],"echo":false}



output holds the events in order. Each event’s kind is display or explicit, and its data is a MIME bundle with text/plain. A value with a renderer adds the renderer’s types, such as image/svg+xml. Returned values carry contents and axis labels, without renderers. Keyed entries that hold functions are omitted. Any other function in a result gives a null value, and output holds its display.
Atoms are encoded directly. Arrays carry shape, row-major data and prototype, including rank-zero arrays. Nested items use the same encoding. A keyed array adds axis_keys: one string list or null per axis. All-unkeyed arrays omit it.
Named dimensions add axis_names: one string or null per axis, e.g. ["city", "month"]. Arrays with no named axes omit it. Encoded arrays in requests take both fields too.



Atom
JSON




Exact integer
Integer, including arbitrary precision


Approximate real
Number with decimal point or exponent


Character
String


Rational
{"rational":["1","3"]}


Complex
{"complex":[1.0,2.0]}


Infinity
{"infinity":1} or {"infinity":-1}


NaN
{"nan":1}



Use the tags for infinities and NaN, never raw NaN or Infinity tokens. Integer inputs stay exact. JavaScript’s JSON.parse rounds integers larger than 2⁵³. Use a parser that keeps integers exact. Error spans are UTF-8 byte ranges into the supplied source. Call sites accompany the original location.




Python’s Worker manages a persistent bpl --worker subprocess with deadlines and a hard-kill fallback.
from basedpl.worker import Worker

with Worker() as w:
    w.eval('v←⍳10')
    r = w.eval('+/v', timeout=2)
    assert r['value'] == 45
w.interrupt() cancels from another thread. Ctrl-C requests cancellation too. Cooperative cancellation preserves the session and completed assignments. If the process doesn’t respond within the grace period, one second by default, Worker kills it and the session is lost. Worker never replays a request. w.diagnostics holds recent stderr. Worker.request(payload, timeout=...) sends any request and supplies its id.

title: Terms
text:
Terms
The Language overview introduces these terms informally, as they come up.
Every value is an atom or an array: atoms are numbers, characters, functions and operators, scalars are arrays of rank 0, units are atoms and scalars, and subjects are all values except functions and operators.



Term
Meaning




value
a number, character, function, operator or array


atom
a value that isn’t an array: a number, character, function or operator


number
an approximate real or complex number, or an exact integer or rational, as Numbers describes


whole
with no fractional part. Integers are whole, as are floats such as 3.0 and ¯3.0


Mathish types
ordinary exact numbers, 64-bit floats and complex numbers with 64-bit parts, under dynamic kinds. Fixed-integer calculations are excluded. Mathish mode applies its conventions when enabled


character
one Unicode character, written in single quotes: 'a'


primitive
a built-in function or operator, written as one glyph: + or /


dfn
a function or operator written in braces, as Dfns describes: {⍵+1}


function
a primitive, train, derived function, or dfn that doesn’t use ⍶ or ⍹, which applies to arguments


operator
a primitive, or a dfn that uses ⍶ or ⍹, which takes operands and derives a function: / derives +/ from +


derived function
a function that an operator derives: +/, or 2↣×


pervasive function
a function that applies to each atom of its arguments, through any nesting: ≥[2 ⊂3] is [3 ⊂4]


array
a rectangular collection of values along zero or more axes


rank
the number of axes: a vector has rank 1, and atoms and scalars have rank 0


vector
an array of rank 1


matrix
an array of rank 2


string
a vector of characters, written in double quotes: "abc"


scalar
an array of rank 0, holding one value: ⊂5 is a scalar holding the number 5, and 5 is a number


unit
a rank-0 value: a number, character, function, operator or scalar


subject
a value that isn’t a function or operator: a number, character or array


item
the value at one position of an array: [1 [2 3]] has the items 1 and [2 3]


position
an index along an axis, counting from 0. Negative positions count from the end


axis
one of the dimensions of an array, numbered from 0. Each axis has a length, and can have a name and keys


key
a string that labels a position along an axis, as Keyed arrays describes


record
a vector with keys, written as key:value items in brackets: ["a":1 "b":2]


cell
a sub-array made of an array’s last k axes, called a k-cell: a matrix’s rows are its 1-cells. A 0-cell is the unit at one position, the atom there or the array there enclosed. When k is at least the array’s rank, the whole array is its one cell


major cell
a cell made of every axis but the first: a matrix’s rows are its major cells


frame
the axes before the cells, with one cell at each position


assembly
building one array from results, one for each position of a frame: the shape is the frame followed by the results’ shape, each result fills its position with its items, and shorter results are padded with fill


function array
an array with a function as an item. Evaluation gives the rule for calling one: 2 [+ ×] 3 is 5 6


map
a call of Each, Rank, an outer product or a stencil, which applies its operand at each position of a frame: to each item, cell, pair of items or window. These are the map’s cells. Evaluation describes how a map calls its operand


fill
the value an operation uses where an array has no item, as when 5↑1 2 gives 1 2 0 0 0. It comes from the array’s prototype: its first item with each number made 0, each character made a space, and each function kept. A call can choose its own fill through ⍠’s options record


selection
values read from an argument together with their places in it, as a list of positions or a function such as 1↓ reads them


glyph
a symbol for a primitive or for syntax, as the glyph reference lists


name
a word that refers to a value, as Syntax describes: x or avg


statement
the code between two newlines or ⋄ separators. Inside brackets and parentheses, these separate rows instead


literal
a number, character, string, ∞, ⍬, or a constant: $t true, $f false or $n NaN


group
brackets, parentheses or braces with what they hold: (1+2), [a b] or {⍵}


token
a glyph, name, literal or group


run
a sequence of tokens with no spaces between them


token separator
⁝ separates tokens without ending a run or continuing a literal strand


strand
subjects side by side, read as a vector without brackets: 1 2 3 is [1 2 3], and a b is [a b]


argument
a subject a function applies to


operand
a value an operator applies to


monadic
taking one argument, or for an operator, one operand: -5 is a monadic call


dyadic
taking two arguments, or for an operator, two operands: 3-5 is a dyadic call


expression
a run, group or statement that ends in a subject


train
a run, group or statement that ends in a function


part
one of the pieces a train is built from: a literal strand, or a token with the operators bound to it, such as 2, +/ or (+×-)


fork
three parts of a train, f g h, giving (f ⍵) g (h ⍵)


tine
one of the two outer parts of a fork


atop
two parts of a train, f g, giving f (g ⍵)


bind
a subject directly before a part, fixing that part’s left argument: 2× is 2↣×, and in 2\|#⊢ the 2 binds \|


fast combination
a combination of functions that BPL computes by an algorithm of its own, in any spelling: 10↑⍋v, ⍟1+x

title: Dfns
text:
A dfn is a function written in braces. ⍵ is its right argument:
{⍵×2}3

6
⍺ is its left argument:
2{⍺+⍵}3

5

title: Dfns
text:
Statements
A dfn returns the value of its last statement. Statements are separated by ⋄ or by line breaks:

{x←≥⍵
 x×2}3

8


The values of earlier statements are discarded:

{1 ⋄ 2}0

2


A statement can run for its side effect alone, such as adding each item to a total:

{s←0
 {s+←⍵}¨⍵
 s}1 2 3

6


A dfn that ends in an assignment returns the assigned value without displaying it:

r←{x←≥⍵}3
r

4

title: Dfns
text:
Scope
Names follow lexical scope. Modified assignment, such as +←, updates the nearest binding of its name, looking outward through enclosing dfns to the top level:

aa←3
bob←{aa+←⍵ ⋄ aa}
bob 5

8


Plain assignment always creates a name local to its dfn:

{gg←1 ⋄ {gg←⍵}¨⍳⍵ ⋄ gg}5

1


A dfn releases each local name after the last statement that reads it. For the rest of the call, the name no longer holds its array. A waiting computation that only the name held then runs with the calls that read it, without being stored first, as Performance describes. A dfn whose text contains ⍎ keeps all its names, because ⍎ can read any of them:

{a←⍵ ⋄ b←a+1 ⋄ b+⍎"a"}5

⍎ that comes from outside the dfn’s text, as an operand or through a name bound outside the dfn, can’t read a name after its last read. It raises VALUE ERROR: “a has no value after its last read in the dfn”.

title: Dfns
text:
Bodies and predicates
; separates a dfn’s bodies. A predicate C? tests the Boolean singleton C. When C is false, the dfn abandons the body and tries the next one. This dfn negates a negative number:

{⍵<0?-⍵;⍵}¯3

3


After a predicate, a body can hold several statements:

{⍵<0?a←-⍵ ⋄ a×2;⍵}¯3

6


A name assigned in one body is still there in the next:

{a←⍵ ⋄ a>9?"big";a>0?"small";"none"}5

small


Every body but the last needs a predicate. If every predicate fails, the call is a DOMAIN error.
An empty body, such as {} or the first body of {⍵≡0?;⍵}, returns no result.

title: Dfns
text:
Arguments
In a call with one argument, ⍺ is absent. An expression that uses an absent ⍺ is evaluated as if ⍺ weren’t there. Called with one argument, {⍺-⍵} negates:

{⍺-⍵}3

¯3


Called with two, the same dfn subtracts:

10{⍺-⍵}3

7


Anything computed only from an absent ⍺ drops out with it:

{2×⍺ - ⍵}3

¯3


In a list, an absent ⍺ leaves no item:

{≢[⍺ ⍵]}3

1ₓ


Any other use, such as x←⍺ or ⍺ as an operand, is a VALUE error.
⍺← gives ⍺ a default. The assignment runs only when ⍺ is absent:

sub←{⍺←10 ⋄ ⍺-⍵}
sub 3
2 sub 3

7


¯1


Valences, ⊘, joins a monadic function and a dyadic function into one.

title: Dfns
text:
Recursion
∇ calls the current dfn. This dfn is factorial:

{⍵=0?1;⍵×∇≤⍵}5

120


A call to ∇ that is the last thing its body does reuses the current frame.

title: Dfns
text:
Operators
A dfn that uses ⍶, its left operand, is a monadic operator. twice applies its operand two times:

twice←{⍶ ⍶ ⍵}
-twice 3

3


A dfn that also uses ⍹, its right operand, is a dyadic operator. This one applies ⍶ between ⍺ and ⍹ ⍵:

2 +{⍺ ⍶ ⍹ ⍵}- 3

¯1


⍢ refers to the current operator, for recursion with new operands.

title: Dfns
text:
Error guards
An error guard kinds::handler makes the dfn return handler when an error of one of the named kinds happens after it, in any later statement or body. ÷"a" raises a DOMAIN error:

{"DOMAIN"::0 ⋄ ÷⍵}"a"

0


In the handler, $e is the caught error, as a record. Its message says what went wrong:

{∞::$e.message ⋄ ÷⍵}"a"

expected numeric elements


•signal raises an error, with a message on its left. The kind can be the program’s own, and a guard catches it by name:

{"NOTFOUND"::$e.message ⋄ "no such user" •signal "NOTFOUND"}0

no such user

title: Dfns
text:
Design
BPL’s dfns come from Dyalog APL, with three rules from BQN’s blocks: the last statement gives the result, predicates choose between bodies separated by ;, and an absent left argument drops out of the expression, as BQN’s 𝕨 does.
In Dyalog APL, a statement that isn’t an assignment returns at once. Running a statement only for its side effect needs a workaround.
Marshall Lochbaum’s five-year review of BQN’s design criticises two BQN features that BPL leaves out: choosing a body by argument count, which Valences covers in BPL, and block headers. The review finds that BQN’s rule for 𝕨, which BPL adopts, makes ambivalent code easier to write than tacit combinators do.
Unlike the review, BPL still lets special names decide what braces define. Braces whose body uses ⍶ or ⍹ define an operator. Other braces define a function.
Unlike a BQN block, a dfn keeps one scope across its bodies, as Dyalog APL’s guards do.

title: •js — JavaScript functions
text:
•js — JavaScript functions
•js source returns a BPL function that calls the JavaScript function source evaluates to. f Y calls it with Y, and X f Y with X then Y. For example, after h←•js "Math.hypot", 3 h 4 is 5. Only the browser build has •js. A page that runs BPL can also give it JavaScript functions and values by name, with Session.bind.
Arguments cross into JavaScript, and results come back, as this table shows. •canvas, Session.eval and Session.bind follow it too.







BPL

{shape, data}. data is a Float32Array for 32-bit floats and complex numbers with 32-bit parts, and a Float64Array for other approximate and fractional numbers. For integers, it’s a Uint8Array, Int16Array, Int32Array or BigInt64Array, at the width BPL stores them. Complex numbers are their real and imaginary parts in turn, with a last axis of length 2.

A JavaScript function becomes a BPL function. undefined and null give no result.

text:
•distribution — Distributions

quantile p inverts the CDF. cdf⁻¹ is quantile. quantile⁻¹ is cdf.

d←•distribution "normal"
d.cdf 0                         ⍝ 0.5

b.quantile 0.5                  ⍝ 5ₓ

title: •literal — Literals
text:
•literal — Literals
•literal⁻¹ Y writes Y as BPL source text, in the notation that display uses. •literal text reads such text back into its value without running code. The text may hold literals and the functions that •literal⁻¹ writes: ⍴, ⊂, ,, : and •ucs. Nested, keyed and exact values read back unchanged. Floats carry the marker of their width, ₚ, ₛ or ₕ, so the text reads back the same at any default width. •hash •literal⁻¹ Y hashes any array.
•literal⁻¹ 2 3⍴⍳6              ⍝ "[0 1 2⋄3 4 5]ₚ"
•literal "[1 [2 3ₓ] ""ab""]"   ⍝ [1 [2 3ₓ] "ab"]
Errors: DOMAIN when the argument of •literal⁻¹ holds a function or an operator, and when the text given to •literal holds a name, another function or more than one value; SYNTAX for text that doesn’t parse.

title: •delay — Delay
text:
•delay — Delay
•delay s pauses for s seconds and returns the seconds it actually waited, which aren’t displayed. An interrupt stops it, and •delay ∞ waits for one.
Errors: DOMAIN for a negative number of seconds, or an s that isn’t a number.
The browser build has no •delay.

title: •detach — Detach
text:
•detach — Detach
•detach x gives x with every ∂ tag removed. Under ∂, no derivative flows back through the result, at any level of nested ∂. Outside ∂, •detach x gives x. Nested arrays and records are detached throughout.
{+/⍵×⍵}∂ 1 2 3            ⍝ 2 4 6
{+/⍵×•detach ⍵}∂ 1 2 3    ⍝ 1 2 3
{⍵×•detach ⍵}∂∂ 3         ⍝ 0
A value computed before a ∂ call is already a constant inside it. •detach is needed only where the cut falls inside one call: a term that comes from the argument but must carry no gradient, such as a target built from the same parameters, or statistics treated as constants.
Apply •detach to a computation’s inputs rather than to its result. net •detach θ runs net on plain values, at the cost of running it without ∂, as PyTorch’s torch.no_grad() does. •detach net θ runs net under ∂ first and then discards its derivative, as .detach() does. Only the first form saves the work.
A common cut falls on a shift that keeps a result finite. Logsumexp subtracts the largest item before * and adds it back after ⍟. The shift drops out of the gradient. Detaching the input of ⌈/, as here, gives the same gradient and keeps ∂ from differentiating ⌈/:
lse←{m←⌈/•detach ⍵ ⋄ m+⍟+/*⍵-m}
lse 1000 1001 1002        ⍝ 1002.407606
lse∂ 1 2 3                ⍝ 0.09003057317 0.2447284711 0.6652409558
∂ differentiates a function.

title: •plot — Plots
text:
•plot — Plots
X •plot Y returns a plot spec: a keyed vector holding the data Y and the settings X. Its renderer displays the spec as an SVG chart. Plain text on the left is shorthand for mark. Plots shows each mark and setting with examples.
The structure of Y chooses the series and axes:

A vector plots its values against 0…n-1.
A keyed vector of numbers uses its keys as x labels.
A matrix plots one series per row. Row keys name the series. Column keys label x.
With the cell mark, each row of a matrix is a row of cells, coloured by value. Row keys label the rows, and row 0 is at the top.
A table, a keyed vector of equal-length columns, plots each column as a series. A column named x supplies the x values.
A vector or matrix of plots draws a figure.

text:
•rename — Rename
to •rename from moves from to to and returns to, which isn’t displayed. Both must be on the same filesystem.
Errors: IO for file errors.

title: •vfi — Numeric input
text:
•vfi — Numeric input
•vfi text returns two vectors, [valid numbers], for the whitespace-separated fields of text. An invalid field has the flag 0ₓ and the value zero. The zero takes the other values’ type wherever it keeps its value there, as a reader’s fill does: •vfi "2ₓ nope" gives [[1 0]ₓ;[2 0]ₓ]. Fields are parsed as numbers, never executed.
Fields take BPL’s written forms of numbers, with plain letters or subscripts. •vfi reads back the numbers that ⍕ displays:
•vfi ⍕1r3 1j2 1e20   ⍝ [[1 1 1]ₓ [1ᵣ3 1ⱼ2 1ₑ20]]
separators •vfi text splits on each character in separators instead. It trims whitespace around fields. An empty field is a valid 0. Numeric input covers it.
Errors: DOMAIN when either argument is not text.

title: •time — Timing
text:
•time — Timing
•time t gives the seconds since the moment t. Moments count seconds from the Unix epoch, as •date reads and writes them. •time 0 is the current moment. t←•time 0 starts a timer, and •time t then gives the seconds since it started.
F •time x calls each function in F on x for about 0.1 s. The result is each function’s fastest time per call in seconds, with the shape and keys of F. With F←["sum":+/ "max":⌈/], F •time x labels each time. Put a single function in brackets, as in [f] •time x. A function before •time takes the result of •time x as its argument, so f •time x times nothing. Time a dyadic function with its left argument bound, as in 2↣⍴. Timing has examples.
Errors: DOMAIN for a left argument that holds anything but functions, or a t that isn’t a number. An error from a timed function stops the timing.

title: •storage — Storage
text:
•storage — Storage
•storage Y gives a record of how the items of Y are held. It reads no items, and a pending call stays pending.

kind names the storage: "bool", "integer", "float64", "float32", "float16", "complex128", "complex64", "character" or "mixed". An atom gives its own kind. That can also be "rational", for an exact rational or an integer beyond 64 bits, or "function". Compact storage holds items of one kind. "integer" covers integers of every width. Mixed storage keeps each item’s kind. Boxed display marks the same storage on its bottom edge. Storage describes each storage.
pending is $t while fusion hasn’t yet run the call that computes the items.
view is $t when Y reads another array’s items, as a reshape does.
active counts the levels of ∂ whose tags Y carries. Under ∂, kind names the storage of the value being differentiated.

•storage 1.5 2.5             ⍝ ["kind":"float64" "pending":$f "view":$f "active":0ₓ]
(•storage 2 3⍴⍳6ₓ).view       ⍝ $t
y←1.5+¿200000⍴0
(•storage y).pending         ⍝ $t

title: •path — Paths
text:
•path — Paths
•path text splits a path into a record of its parts, named after Rust’s: parent, stem, extension and name. It never reads the disk. The option absolute first joins a relative path to the working directory, as Rust’s std::path::absolute does, without resolving links. •path⁻¹ joins parent, stem and extension into a path, and ignores name. An array of paths gives a record of arrays.
•path "data/sales.csv"                            ⍝ ["parent":"data" "stem":"sales" "extension":"csv" "name":"sales.csv"]
{⍵.extension←"tsv" ⋄ ⍵}@•path "data/sales.csv"   ⍝ "data/sales.tsv"
Errors: DOMAIN when a path isn’t text, for an unknown part, or for an absolute path that is empty or has no working directory to join.

title: •index — Fresh indices
text:
•index — Fresh indices
•index n gives ⍳n along an axis with a fresh name. stem •index n starts the name with the text stem. The name is _, the stem, · and a random part of 64 bits written as 13 digits, as in _b·k3f9q2m7x1c0p. Two calls give different names, except with a chance of about one in 10¹⁹. •index maps over an array of numbers, with the same stem for each. It also maps over a nested array: one call can make every index that a formula needs. A keyed shape gives a record of indices with the shape’s keys. Plain •index⍴x, with no stem, is the usual form:
x←2 3⍴⍳6 ⋄ [[n i] h]←•index[⍴x 4]
⍴:x.[n i]×h                ⍝ [2 3 4]ₓ
k←["n":2 "i":3]⍴⍳6
•index⍴k                   ⍝ ["n":[0 1]ₓ "i":[0 1 2]ₓ]
A name that starts with _ is hidden. Plain display leaves hidden axis names out. Any key or name that starts with _ and contains · displays up to its last ·, then …. Box mode, ⍴ and error messages show a fresh name as _b·…. To keep a long key or name of your own short on screen, start it with _ and put a · before the part to leave out: ["_note·long description":3] displays as ["_note·…":3]. •literal⁻¹ writes every name in full. A hidden name meets a visible one as if that axis had no name, and the result keeps the visible name:
i←•index 3 ⋄ v←⍳["v":3]
i          ⍝ 0 1 2
⍴i         ⍝ ["_·…":3]ₓ
⍴i+v       ⍝ ["v":3]ₓ
Indices with different names build a grid, in arithmetic and in selection. An index used twice pairs with itself. Here x.[i]-x.[j] holds the difference between every pair of items of x, and m.[i i] is the diagonal of m:
x←10 20 40 ⋄ [i j]←•index 3 3
⌈/,|x.[i]-x.[j]      ⍝ 30
m←[1 2 3⋄4 5 6⋄7 8 9]
+/m.[i i]            ⍝ 15
Indices name the axes of a formula, as einsum’s letters do. In this product, +.×⍠k sums along k, the index that both operands share. b and o build the result’s grid. ⍉⁻¹ reorders its axes by name:
xu←[2 3]⍴⍳6ₓ ⋄ wu←[3 4]⍴⍳12ₓ
[b o k]←•index 2 4 3
y←xu.[b k]+.×⍠k⁝wu.[k o]
∧/,y=xu+.×wu                 ⍝ $t
∧/, [o b]⍉⁻¹y = ⍉xu+.×wu     ⍝ $t
Models in index notation builds a neural network and a transformer’s attention with indices.
Names from •index can’t collide with the names on a caller’s data. ⍳["i":n] gives a name that the caller chooses.
∂ of a dfn that uses •index runs from a program, as ∂ of any other dfn does. Each call’s result still has new names. A map calls such a dfn once on all its cells, as Evaluation describes for any dfn. The cells share each name that the dfn draws. Where the dfn’s result holds one of those names, the map calls the dfn once for each cell instead. Each cell’s result then has names of its own.
Errors: DOMAIN for a stem that isn’t text.

title: •normalize — Unicode normalization
text:
•normalize — Unicode normalization
•normalize text puts text into Unicode normalization form NFC. NFC uses one code point for a letter and its accent wherever Unicode has one. form •normalize text names the form: "NFC", "NFD", "NFKC" or "NFKD". NFD writes each accented letter as a base letter followed by combining marks. The K forms also replace compatibility characters, such as the ligature ﬁ, with ordinary ones.
•ucs "NFD" •normalize "é"   ⍝ [101 769]ₓ
"NFKC" •normalize "ﬁ"       ⍝ "fi"
Errors: DOMAIN for an unknown form, or an argument that isn’t text.

X⍸Y counts how many boundaries in sorted X are less than or equal to each value of Y.

Splitting, naming and merging axes
A nested item splits one input axis into several axes. Here the last axis of length 8 becomes two axes of lengths 2 and 4, named "group" and "offset". Dyadic operator ⌺ (Stencil)
A window is a section of an array around one position. Stencil applies its left operand to each window, with that position at the centre. Its right operand gives the window’s size. At the edges, missing items use fill: zero for these numeric arrays. Enclosing each window shows what the operand receives:

title: Automatic differentiation
text:
f∂X gives the derivative of f at X. ∂ works by running f. It differentiates through the primitives that f calls, inside dfns, trains and operators alike. A function needs no special form to be differentiated. ⊼ squares its argument. +/⊼ sums the squares:
⊼∂3                          ⍝ 6
(+/⊼)∂ 1 2 3                 ⍝ 2 4 6
The ∂ page lists what ∂ differentiates and the errors it gives.


The Jacobian of f at X holds the derivative of each item of f X with respect to each number in X. f∂X gives it, with the keys, axis names and nesting of the outer product (f X)×⊗X. A function that gives a number has a Jacobian with X’s structure: its gradient. A record argument gives a record gradient, with the record’s keys. cart converts polar coordinates to Cartesian ones. Its Jacobian has a row for each result and a column for each argument:
cart←{[r t]←⍵ ⋄ [r×2○t r×1○t]} ⋄ cart∂ 2 0.5   ⍝ [0.8775825619 ¯0.9588510772⋄0.4794255386 1.755165124]
p←["w":2 "b":1] ⋄ {3×⍵.w + ⍵.b}∂ p               ⍝ ["w":3 "b":1]
W f∂ X differentiates W f X with respect to X. The left argument holds what isn’t differentiated, such as training data:
3 {⍺×⍵×⍵}∂ 2                ⍝ 12
A JVP is the derivative of f at x in a direction t. {f x+⍵×t}∂0 computes it by differentiating along one number. A vector–Jacobian product multiplies a vector u by the Jacobian. {+/u×f⍵}∂ x computes it by differentiating a sum. Neither builds the Jacobian. With t and u both 1 0, the JVP gives the Jacobian’s first column. The vector–Jacobian product gives its first row:
f←{[x y]←⍵ ⋄ [x×y x+y]} ⋄ x←2 3
f∂ x                        ⍝ [3 2⋄1 1]
t←1 0 ⋄ {f x+⍵×t}∂0         ⍝ 3 1
u←1 0 ⋄ {+/u×f⍵}∂ x         ⍝ 3 2
For a function that works item by item, such as the sine 1○, f∂⍤0 gives the derivative at each item. Differentiating along one number gives the same values in one pass:
x←0 0.5 1
1○∂⍤0 x                     ⍝ 1 0.8775825619 0.5403023059
{1○x+⍵}∂0                   ⍝ 1 0.8775825619 0.5403023059
f∂∂ is ∂ applied to f∂. It gives second and mixed derivatives, such as the matrix of mixed derivatives of ×/, the product of the items. Exact numbers give exact derivatives:
{⍵×⍵×⍵}∂∂∂2                  ⍝ 6
×/∂∂ 2 3                     ⍝ [0 1⋄1 0]
⊼∂3ₓ                         ⍝ 6ₓ



Where X holds one number, ∂ runs f once, in forward mode. Every value that depends on X carries its derivative with respect to X beside it, as a dual number. ∂ starts the pass by making X a dual whose derivative is 1. A call on duals gives a dual. A pervasive function, such as × or *, finds its result’s derivative by the chain rule, from a table of its partial derivatives. ⍺×⍵ has the partials ⍵ and ⍺. *⍵ has the partial *⍵, its own result. ∂ returns the derivative that the final result carries.
Each ∂ call tags the duals it makes. A call reads only the derivatives with its own tag. Under nested ∂, as in {⍵×⍵×⍵}∂∂∂2, a value is a dual of a dual of a dual. Julia’s ForwardDiff tags its dual numbers in the same way.
Functions that move items, such as reshape, transpose, take and windows, move each item’s derivative with the item. Comparisons, floor, ⍳, grade and other functions whose results are counts, positions or Booleans give results with no derivative.



Forward mode takes one pass for each number in X. A network with a million parameters would take a million passes. Where X holds more than one number, ∂ instead runs f once with a record in place of each derivative. A record’s items are never computed. Each call on a record adds a linear step to it, built from the same partial derivatives that forward mode uses. The steps are few: scaling by a coefficient, adding, copying from positions, broadcasting, folding by +, and matrix products with a constant. When f returns, the record holds the linearisation of f at X. That’s the linear map from a small change in X to the change it causes in f X.
∂ then reads the Jacobian from the record. A run through the record backwards, through each step’s transpose in reverse order, gives one row of the Jacobian. A run forwards gives one column. ∂ takes whichever direction needs fewer runs. A function that gives a number, such as a loss, needs one backward run. Its gradient costs a small multiple of one run of f, however many numbers X holds. Dex and JAX also build reverse mode as the transpose of a linearisation. One set of tangent rules then serves both modes.
Each linear step has one transpose:







Step
Transpose




Scaling by a coefficient
Scaling by the same coefficient


Adding two values
The same gradient to each value


A broadcast
A sum over the broadcast axes


A fold by + along an axis
A broadcast along that axis


A copy that reads each item at most once, such as a transpose, reverse, take or drop
A copy back through the inverse map


A sum over windows that move by 1
A sliding sum


Windows that move by more than 1
Each window’s gradient, added back where the window read


A selection that can repeat positions
An accumulation into those positions


A matrix product with a constant
A matrix product with the constant’s transpose



The transposes work on whole arrays, as the steps do. The transpose of a selection adds each gradient into the position that it was read from. It never builds an array of zeros with a one at each position read. In this example, 3↕ gives windows of 3. The first function reads item 0 twice and never reads item 1. In the second, the middle items appear in more of the windows:
0 0 2 {+/⊼⍵.[⍺]}∂ 1 2 3     ⍝ 4 0 6
{+/,⊼3↕⍵}∂ 1 2 3 4 5        ⍝ 2 8 18 16 10
Folds and matrix functions have rules of their own. ×/ divides the product by each item to find that item’s derivative, with zeros counted apart. ⌈/ and ⌊/ take the derivative of the item that they pick. ⌹ and the determinant -.× take their derivatives from one factorization of the matrix.
The record keeps the values that its steps need, such as the coefficients of its scalings, until ∂ returns. Its memory grows with the work that f does.



f∂←g attaches g as the derivative of f. g is a JVP rule: T g X gives the derivative of f at X in the direction T. Forward mode calls g with the tangent as T. Reverse mode records the steps that g takes on T, then transposes them, as JAX transposes a custom_jvp rule. One rule serves both modes. A straight-through estimator, which treats rounding as if its derivative were 1, is such a rule:
r←{⍵×⍵} ⋄ r∂←{⍺×2×⍵}
{1+r⍵}∂3                    ⍝ 6
ste←{⌊⍵} ⋄ ste∂←{⍺}
{+/ste⍵×2}∂ 1.5 2.5         ⍝ 2 2
•detach X gives X with every derivative removed. ∂ then treats it as a constant, as JAX treats the result of stop_gradient. ⊢×•detach multiplies its argument by a detached copy of itself. Its derivative at 3 is the copy’s value, 3, where ⊼∂3 gives 6:
(⊢×•detach)∂3                ⍝ 3
A value that f writes to a name outside itself loses its derivatives when ∂ returns. A function gives the same values with and without ∂.



Without a program, ∂ builds its duals or its record afresh on every call, through the interpreter. A training loop calls ∂ hundreds of times, with arguments of the same types and shapes. This loop fits a network with 16 tanh units (7○) to 64 points of sin 3x (1○3×x), in 200 steps of gradient descent on a record of parameters:
x←⍳64 ÷ 63 ⋄ y←1○3×x
loss←{[x y]←⍺ ⋄ [w b v c]←⍵ ⋄ h←7○b(+⍤1)x×⊗w ⋄ +/÷≢ ⊼y-c+h+.×v}

∂ runs from a program. The first call with given argument types and shapes traces the function. The function runs on traced values, which have a type and a shape but no items. Each call on a traced value works out the type and shape of its result, and adds a step to the program. The derivative’s records and transposes run on traced values too. The program holds the whole call: the function’s value and its derivative together. JAX traces a Python function into a jaxpr in the same way.
Later calls with the same argument types and shapes replay the program on their arguments, without running the function. The replay runs each chain of elementwise steps as one stage, a block of items at a time. A stage folds its last step’s items as it computes them. Its intermediate results exist only one block at a time. Once a stage is large enough, or runs again, BPL compiles it to machine code with Cranelift, if its steps can compile. The browser build has no compiler. It runs every stage on the interpreter’s kernels. tinygrad’s TinyJit replays the kernels of an earlier call in the same way. •explain shows whether a call built a program or replayed one:
sq←{+/⊼⍵} ⋄ g←sq∂ 1 2 3
(•explain "sq∂ 4 5 6").programs.event      ⍝ ["replayed"]
(•explain "sq∂ 4 5 6 7").programs.event    ⍝ ["built"]
The second call replays the program that the first call built. Four numbers need a program of their own.
A dfn keeps its programs with its definition. Any other function, such as a train, keeps them by its structure for the rest of the session. The structure leaves out the arrays that the function binds, which become inputs, as a dfn’s free names do. So +/w×⊢ replays its program when w holds new values of the same type and shape:
w←1 2 3 ⋄ g←(+/w×⊢)∂ 4 5 6
w←7 8 9 ⋄ (•explain "(+/w×⊢)∂ 4 5 6").programs.event   ⍝ ["replayed"]
A trace stops at anything that a program can’t hold: output or another effect, a random draw, ⍎, a read of a differentiated value, as a guard on one makes, or a call that no plan covers. ∂ then runs the call through duals and records. ∂ keeps the stop for those argument types and shapes. •explain gives the reason in its stopped rows:
pos←{+/⍵ > 0 ? +/⊼⍵ ; 0}
(•explain "pos∂ 1 2 3").stopped.reason    ⍝ ["a read of a traced value"]
Each replay reads the current value of every name that the function reads from outside its body, and of every array that a function other than a dfn binds. A name or an array read as positions, a count or a guard’s condition is part of the program itself. A replay checks its value. A new value traces the function again.
A program fixes every type before it runs. Under the default dynamic kinds, a result’s type can depend on its values: √ of a negative number gives a complex number. A trace stops at such a call. Under static kinds, which •prefs ["kinds":"static"] sets, every type follows from the argument types. The same call then traces. Static kinds are the setting for work where speed matters.
roots←{+/√⍵}
(•explain "roots∂ 1 2 3").stopped.reason  ⍝ ["a result whose type depends on values"]
Write a function for ∂ under static kinds, with each branch as Agenda (⍚) or Under at positions (f@[p]) rather than a guard. A guard reads a differentiated value to pick one body for the whole call, which a program can’t hold. ⍚ and @ pick items within whole arrays. Today they also stop a trace where their choice or their values come from differentiated values. ∂ still gives the right result there, more slowly. Tracing them is planned, as “Not built yet” describes.



Index notation writes the formula for one element with named indices. BPL runs the formula once, on whole arrays. Indexing and •index describe it. ∂ differentiates index notation as it differentiates any other code. This matrix product, written with indices, has the same gradient as +.×:

A + fold over named axes of a product, where both operands step along every folded axis, runs as a matrix product +.×. The folds in its gradient run as products where they meet the same condition.

A gradient costs a small multiple of one run of the function, whatever the number of variables.

One rule for each primitive serves both modes.
Nested ∂ never confuses its levels.

title: Automatic differentiation
text:
The Jacobian of f at X holds the derivative of each item of f X with respect to each number in X. f∂X gives it, with the keys, axis names and nesting of the outer product (f X)×⊗X. A function that gives a number has a Jacobian with X’s structure: its gradient. A record argument gives a record gradient, with the record’s keys. cart converts polar coordinates to Cartesian ones. Its Jacobian has a row for each result and a column for each argument:
cart←{[r t]←⍵ ⋄ [r×2○t r×1○t]} ⋄ cart∂ 2 0.5   ⍝ [0.8775825619 ¯0.9588510772⋄0.4794255386 1.755165124]
p←["w":2 "b":1] ⋄ {3×⍵.w + ⍵.b}∂ p               ⍝ ["w":3 "b":1]
W f∂ X differentiates W f X with respect to X. The left argument holds what isn’t differentiated, such as training data:
3 {⍺×⍵×⍵}∂ 2                ⍝ 12
A JVP is the derivative of f at x in a direction t. {f x+⍵×t}∂0 computes it by differentiating along one number. A vector–Jacobian product multiplies a vector u by the Jacobian. {+/u×f⍵}∂ x computes it by differentiating a sum. Neither builds the Jacobian. With t and u both 1 0, the JVP gives the Jacobian’s first column. The vector–Jacobian product gives its first row:
f←{[x y]←⍵ ⋄ [x×y x+y]} ⋄ x←2 3
f∂ x                        ⍝ [3 2⋄1 1]
t←1 0 ⋄ {f x+⍵×t}∂0         ⍝ 3 1
u←1 0 ⋄ {+/u×f⍵}∂ x         ⍝ 3 2
For a function that works item by item, such as the sine 1○, f∂⍤0 gives the derivative at each item. Differentiating along one number gives the same values in one pass:
x←0 0.5 1
1○∂⍤0 x                     ⍝ 1 0.8775825619 0.5403023059
{1○x+⍵}∂0                   ⍝ 1 0.8775825619 0.5403023059
f∂∂ is ∂ applied to f∂. It gives second and mixed derivatives, such as the matrix of mixed derivatives of ×/, the product of the items. Exact numbers give exact derivatives:
{⍵×⍵×⍵}∂∂∂2                  ⍝ 6
×/∂∂ 2 3                     ⍝ [0 1⋄1 0]
⊼∂3ₓ                         ⍝ 6ₓ

title: Automatic differentiation
text:
Where X holds one number, ∂ runs f once, in forward mode. Every value that depends on X carries its derivative with respect to X beside it, as a dual number. ∂ starts the pass by making X a dual whose derivative is 1. A call on duals gives a dual. A pervasive function, such as × or *, finds its result’s derivative by the chain rule, from a table of its partial derivatives. ⍺×⍵ has the partials ⍵ and ⍺. *⍵ has the partial *⍵, its own result. ∂ returns the derivative that the final result carries.
Each ∂ call tags the duals it makes. A call reads only the derivatives with its own tag. Under nested ∂, as in {⍵×⍵×⍵}∂∂∂2, a value is a dual of a dual of a dual. Julia’s ForwardDiff tags its dual numbers in the same way.
Functions that move items, such as reshape, transpose, take and windows, move each item’s derivative with the item. Comparisons, floor, ⍳, grade and other functions whose results are counts, positions or Booleans give results with no derivative.

title: Automatic differentiation
text:
Forward mode takes one pass for each number in X. A network with a million parameters would take a million passes. Where X holds more than one number, ∂ instead runs f once with a record in place of each derivative. A record’s items are never computed. Each call on a record adds a linear step to it, built from the same partial derivatives that forward mode uses. The steps are few: scaling by a coefficient, adding, copying from positions, broadcasting, folding by +, and matrix products with a constant. When f returns, the record holds the linearisation of f at X. That’s the linear map from a small change in X to the change it causes in f X.
∂ then reads the Jacobian from the record. A run through the record backwards, through each step’s transpose in reverse order, gives one row of the Jacobian. A run forwards gives one column. ∂ takes whichever direction needs fewer runs. A function that gives a number, such as a loss, needs one backward run. Its gradient costs a small multiple of one run of f, however many numbers X holds. Dex and JAX also build reverse mode as the transpose of a linearisation. One set of tangent rules then serves both modes.
Each linear step has one transpose:







Step
Transpose




Scaling by a coefficient
Scaling by the same coefficient


Adding two values
The same gradient to each value


A broadcast
A sum over the broadcast axes


A fold by + along an axis
A broadcast along that axis


A copy that reads each item at most once, such as a transpose, reverse, take or drop
A copy back through the inverse map


A sum over windows that move by 1
A sliding sum


Windows that move by more than 1
Each window’s gradient, added back where the window read


A selection that can repeat positions
An accumulation into those positions


A matrix product with a constant
A matrix product with the constant’s transpose



The transposes work on whole arrays, as the steps do. The transpose of a selection adds each gradient into the position that it was read from. It never builds an array of zeros with a one at each position read. In this example, 3↕ gives windows of 3. The first function reads item 0 twice and never reads item 1. In the second, the middle items appear in more of the windows:
0 0 2 {+/⊼⍵.[⍺]}∂ 1 2 3     ⍝ 4 0 6
{+/,⊼3↕⍵}∂ 1 2 3 4 5        ⍝ 2 8 18 16 10
Folds and matrix functions have rules of their own. ×/ divides the product by each item to find that item’s derivative, with zeros counted apart. ⌈/ and ⌊/ take the derivative of the item that they pick. ⌹ and the determinant -.× take their derivatives from one factorization of the matrix.
The record keeps the values that its steps need, such as the coefficients of its scalings, until ∂ returns. Its memory grows with the work that f does.

title: Automatic differentiation
text:

{1+r⍵}∂3                    ⍝ 6
ste←{⌊⍵} ⋄ ste∂←{⍺}

A value that f writes to a name outside itself loses its derivatives when ∂ returns. A function gives the same values with and without ∂.

title: Models in index notation
text:
Index notation writes the formula for one item of a result, with a named index for each of its axes. BPL runs the formula once, on whole arrays, and ∂ differentiates it. Tacit code stays BPL’s main style: a plain matrix product reads better as x+.×w than in any index form. Index notation helps where leading axes and Rank line up a formula’s axes badly, as in attention’s heads and causal mask, a convolution’s stride and window, or one step of Gaussian elimination.


A formula in index notation takes three steps:

Make the indices. •index gives ⍳n along a fresh hidden axis name. It maps over a nested shape, so [[n i] h]←•index[⍴x ≢b] makes an index for each axis of x and one for the length of b.
Select with them. x.[n i] holds the items of x along axes named by n and i.
Name the axis that each fold removes, as in +/⍠i.

Indices pair by name. The same index pairs with itself. Different indices build a grid. A matrix product sums along the index that its two operands share. Here k pairs the columns of xu with the rows of wu, and +/⍠k sums along it. b and o build the result’s grid. The inner product along k, +.×⍠k, writes the same contraction. The examples below use it:
xu←[2 3]⍴⍳6ₓ ⋄ wu←[3 4]⍴⍳12ₓ ⋄ [b o k]←•index 2 4 3
y←+/⍠k⁝xu.[b k]×wu.[k o]
∧/,y=xu+.×wu                   ⍝ $t
∧/,y=xu.[b k]+.×⍠k⁝wu.[k o]     ⍝ $t
Each index has its length from the start. BPL doesn’t infer a range from the reads that use it.



This network has one hidden layer of tanh units (7○) and fits y from x by mean squared error. p holds its parameters. mlp is the tacit form, where b(+⍤1) adds the bias to each row. In the index form, mlpi, n names the samples, i the inputs and h the hidden units. Each line of mlpi gives its formula for one sample and one unit. a is the tanh of the bias at h plus the sum over i of x at n i times w at i h. Both forms give the same loss and the same gradient:
•prefs ["seed":42]
x←¯0.5+¿[64 8]⍴0 ⋄ y←1○+/x

  h←7○b(+⍤1)x+.×w

  [x y]←⍺ ⋄ [w b v c]←⍵
  [[n i] h]←•index[⍴x ≢b]

The index form runs at about the tacit form’s speed, forward and under ∂. BPL reads x.[n i] through its indices as a map, without copying x. An inner product along a named axis, as in x.[n i]+.×⍠i⁝w.[i h], runs as the matrix product x+.×w. So does a + fold along a named axis of a product, as in +/⍠i⁝x.[n i]×w.[i h]. Attention lets each token of a sequence read from the tokens before it. x holds a batch of 2 sequences of 4 tokens, each with 8 features. wqkv projects each token to a query, a key and a value for each of 2 heads, with 4 features in each head. wo projects the heads back to 8 features. mask stops a token from reading the tokens after it.

In index notation, b names the sequence, t the token, d the feature and u the token that t reads from. r picks the query, key or value, h names the head and j the feature within a head.   e←*s-⌈/s

}
attni←{
  [wqkv wo]←⍺
  [[b t d] u [r h j]]←•index[⍴⍵ (⍴⍵)₁ 1↓⍴wqkv]
  [q k v]←:[r b t h j]⍉⁻¹⍵.[b t d]+.×⍠d⁝wqkv.[d r h j]
  s←mask.[t u] + q.[b t h j]+.×⍠j⁝k.[b u h j] ÷ √≢j
  e←*s-⌈/⍠u⁝s
  o←(e÷+/⍠u⁝e)+.×⍠u⁝v.[b u h j]
  :[b t d]⍉⁻¹+/⍠[h j]o×wo.[j+(≢j)×h d]
}
a←[wqkv wo]attn x ⋄ ai←[wqkv wo]attni x
1E¯12>⌈/,|a-ai                 ⍝ $t
pa←["wqkv":wqkv "wo":wo]
g←{+/, ⊼[⍵.wqkv ⍵.wo]attn⁝x}∂ pa ⋄ gi←{+/, ⊼[⍵.wqkv ⍵.wo]attni⁝x}∂ pa
1E¯12>⌈/,|g.wqkv-gi.wqkv       ⍝ $t
Line by line, in attni:

The projection is one contraction over d. ⍉⁻¹ puts r first by name. : removes the names. [q k v]← then takes the three parts along the first axis. Without names, each part can be read under new indices.
k.[b u h j] reads the keys with u for their token axis. The scores then pair each query token t with each key token u. mask.[t u] adds ¯1E9 wherever u comes after t.
e÷+/⍠u⁝e is the softmax over u. o sums the values over u, each weighted by its share.
wo.[j+(≢j)×h d] reads the row of wo for head h and feature j. BPL reads through positions computed from indices as a map. The fold over [h j] merges the heads. :[b t d]⍉⁻¹ orders the result’s axes and removes their names, to give attn’s plain shape.




No feature of BPL requires names or keys. A function uses them where they express something. Code written for plain data can give other values on named or keyed data, because there the names say which axes align.
•index gives each index a hidden name that is new on every call. A caller’s names can’t collide with it. An index used twice pairs with itself and gives a diagonal, as in m.[i i]. Different names build a grid in any arithmetic, with no ⊗. A length-1 axis expands to match, as elsewhere in BPL. A design where names only labelled axes, and only ⊗ built a grid, would break both. BPL also has no constructor that gives each index an axis by its position in the call, as NumPy’s ix_ does. •index builds the same grids by name.
Each, Rank and Stencil (⌺) need no new syntax. They suit a function written for one cell, including one that branches cell by cell. Index notation suits a formula written for one item, where the axes that pair differ from line to line. BPL’s design followed a close study of Dex, whose index sets informed •index.



Automatic differentiation lists what traced programs don’t cover yet. Two of its items apply to models like these. A program holds one call of ∂: a training step’s update and the loop around it run outside the program. A per-item branch, such as a selector that Agenda (⍚) computes from differentiated values, stops a trace.

title: Models in index notation
text:
A formula in index notation takes three steps:

Make the indices. •index gives ⍳n along a fresh hidden axis name. It maps over a nested shape, so [[n i] h]←•index[⍴x ≢b] makes an index for each axis of x and one for the length of b.
Select with them. x.[n i] holds the items of x along axes named by n and i.
Name the axis that each fold removes, as in +/⍠i.

Indices pair by name. The same index pairs with itself. Different indices build a grid. A matrix product sums along the index that its two operands share. Here k pairs the columns of xu with the rows of wu, and +/⍠k sums along it. b and o build the result’s grid. The inner product along k, +.×⍠k, writes the same contraction. The examples below use it:
xu←[2 3]⍴⍳6ₓ ⋄ wu←[3 4]⍴⍳12ₓ ⋄ [b o k]←•index 2 4 3
y←+/⍠k⁝xu.[b k]×wu.[k o]
∧/,y=xu+.×wu                   ⍝ $t
∧/,y=xu.[b k]+.×⍠k⁝wu.[k o]     ⍝ $t
Each index has its length from the start. BPL doesn’t infer a range from the reads that use it.

title: Models in index notation
text:
This network has one hidden layer of tanh units (7○) and fits y from x by mean squared error. p holds its parameters. mlp is the tacit form, where b(+⍤1) adds the bias to each row. In the index form, mlpi, n names the samples, i the inputs and h the hidden units. Each line of mlpi gives its formula for one sample and one unit. a is the tanh of the bias at h plus the sum over i of x at n i times w at i h. Both forms give the same loss and the same gradient:

  h←7○b(+⍤1)x+.×w
  +/÷≢ ⊼y-c+h+.×v
}

  [[n i] h]←•index[⍴x ≢b]
  a←7○b.[h]+x.[n i]+.×⍠i⁝w.[i h]
  +/÷≢ ⊼y.[n]-c+a+.×⍠h⁝v.[h]

title: Arrays
text: BPL has two kinds of value. Numbers, characters and functions are atoms. An array is a rectangular collection of values, including other arrays. This is the based array model, named in a 1981 paper and popularized by BQN.

title: Arrays
text:
Writing vectors
Write a vector by putting its items in brackets, separated by spaces. An item can be any expression without a space in it, such as a number, a name, ≥x or a string:

x←10
[x ≥x "hi"]

10 11 "hi"


A bracket list is a vector, however many items it has. Shape, monadic ⍴, shows that [5] has one axis of length 1, where the number 5 has none:

⍴[5]
⍴5

[1]ₓ


⍬ₓ


A list of literals can leave its brackets out. Values written side by side form a strand, the same vector as the bracket list:

1 2 3≡[1 2 3]

$t


Names side by side form a strand too:

a←1
b←2
a b

1 2


Matrices are written in brackets too, one row per line. Types of brackets covers this array notation, along with what ; and ⋄ mean inside brackets:

m←[1 2 3
   4 5 6]
m

1 2 3
4 5 6

title: Arrays
text:
Shape and rank
An array’s shape lists the lengths of its axes. Its rank is the number of axes, the tally of its shape. Scalars, vectors and matrices are the arrays of rank 0, 1 and 2. m has two rows and three columns:

⍴m
≢⍴m

[2 3]ₓ


2ₓ


Reshape, dyadic ⍴, builds an array of any shape from the items on its right. ⍳6 counts from 0 to 5:

2 3⍴⍳6ₓ

[0 1 2
 3 4 5]ₓ


An axis can have length 0. This matrix has no rows and three columns:

⍴0 3⍴0

[0 3]ₓ


Ravel, monadic ,, lists the items in row-major order:

,m

1 2 3 4 5 6

title: Arrays
text:
Atoms and scalars
Neither an atom nor a scalar, the array of rank 0, has any axes. Enclose, ⊂, gives a scalar holding its argument:

⍴3
⍴⊂3

⍬ₓ


⍬ₓ


They’re still different values. A scalar is an array with one position, holding the atom:

3≡⊂3

$f


Enclosing always adds a layer, even around an atom. Depth, monadic ≡, counts the layers:

≡3
≡⊂3
≡⊂⊂3

0ₓ


1ₓ


2ₓ


⊂ encloses only subjects. For a function f, the scalar holding it is fᵘ:

≡+ᵘ

1ₓ

title: Arrays
text:
Nesting
The items of an array can be arrays. This vector holds two vectors of different lengths:

n←[[1 2] [3 4 5]]
n

(1 2⋄3 4 5)


First, monadic ↑, gives the first item. Each, ¨, applies a function to every item, here Tally, ≢:

↑n
≢¨n

1 2


[2 3]ₓ


n, a vector of vectors of numbers, has depth 2:

≡n

2ₓ


Arithmetic, Each and indexing keep the container they map over, even a scalar:

⊂3 + 4
-¨⊂3

⊂7


⊂¯3


Rank and the search functions work on whole cells instead, as Rank describes.

title: Arrays
text:
Fill
Every array has a prototype, which gives its fill. The fill is zero for numbers, a space for characters, and a filled copy of the first item for nested arrays. Take, dyadic ↑, pads with fill when it asks for more items than there are:

5↑[1 2]
"<",3↑"ab" , ">"

1 2 0 0 0


<ab >


An empty array keeps its prototype. First of this empty vector gives the fill of 1 2, the first item of the vector it came from:

↑0⍴n

0 0


When results of different lengths are assembled into one array, the shorter ones are padded with fill. ≥⍳ ⍤0 gives one row per count:

≥⍳ ⍤0 [2 4]

1 2 0 0
1 2 3 4


Each keeps the results as separate items instead:

≥⍳ ¨[2 4]

(1 2⋄1 2 3 4)

title: Arrays
text:
Keys
Keys label the positions along an axis. Write them with :, then pick an item by its key with a dot:

T←"x" "y":1 2
T
T.x

["x":1 "y":2]


1


Axes can also have names. A shape with keys names the axes Reshape builds. Axis keys covers keyed arrays in full:

M←["city":2 "month":3]⍴⍳6ₓ
⍴M

["city":2 "month":3]ₓ

title: Arrays
text:
Functions in arrays
An array can hold functions. fs is a vector of three:

fs←[+ × ÷]
fs

[+ × ÷]


Selecting an item gives back a function you can call. A subscript selects one position:

2 fs₁ 3

6


Pick, ⊃, First, ↑, and Index, ⌷, with a single position also return stored functions. ↑⌽fs is the last one:

div←↑⌽fs
6 div 3

2


A list can mix functions with other values, including a vector of functions as one item:

mixed←[[1 2 3] + ×]
≢mixed
≢[fs ÷]

3ₓ


2ₓ


Successive Picks go down into nested arrays. Empty coordinates return the argument unchanged:

x←[[+ ×] [- ÷]]
f←1⊃0⊃x
2 f 3
⍬⊃n ≡ n

6


$t


A dfn can return a function it selects. Agenda selects one and calls it in one step:

g←{1⊃⍵}fs
2 g 3

6


An array that holds a function as an item is callable. Each function gets the whole arguments, and each other item is its own result:

2 fs 8

10 16 0.25


The results take the array’s shape and keys as their frame, as Rank’s results do. A keyed array of aggregations gives a keyed result, and through Rank it gives one row of results for each row of its argument:

stats←["mean":+/÷≢ "max":⌈/]
stats 3 1 4 1 5
stats⍤1[3 1 4⋄1 5 9]

["mean":2.8 "max":5]


       mean max
2.666666667   4
          5   9


Results of different shapes pad with fill:

[⍳ ⊢] 3

0 1 2
3 0 0


Only direct items count. A scalar that holds a function, such as -ᵘ, calls it, and its empty frame adds no axis. An enclosed function array holds an array, so (⊂fs) 2 is a strand:

-ᵘ 3
(⊂fs) 2

¯3


[⊂[+ × ÷] 2]


A function array acts as a function only where a subject follows it. Elsewhere it’s an array, so ≢fs counts its items. Binding gives the rule, and Operators and operands says which operators call the array:

≢fs

3ₓ


Function items are shared handles, not source text. Reshape, selection, catenation and the other structural functions move them without running them. Display prints each function as its source. A native function with no source spelling, such as a generator’s roll, prints in ⟨…⟩. A function’s fill is the function itself, which Take shows:

5↑fs

[+ × ÷ + +]


Two functions match when they’re built from matching parts. A primitive matches itself, as does a derived function such as +/, however many times either is written. A dfn matches only itself. Two separately written {⍵} don’t match, even though they do the same thing. Functions have no ordering, and Grade and Interval Index reject them.

[+]≡[+]
[+/]≡[+/]
h←{⍵}
[h]≡[h]
[{⍵}]≡[{⍵}]

$t


$t


$t


$f


A dfn can return a function. A local function it captures works while the call that defined it is still running. Returning it, or storing it anywhere that outlives the call, including inside an array or an empty prototype, is a DOMAIN error.
In Python, arrays of functions work as Callable functions describes.

title: Dyalog sessions
text:
Import Apl and AplError from basedpl.dyalog. Sessions return Dyalog output or JSON-converted Python values, not BPL arrays. Importing this module does not start Dyalog or register notebook magics.
Install Dyalog separately. The examples use a local interpreter and run with nbdev-test --flags dyalog. The default test run skips them.
from fastcore.test import *

title: Dyalog sessions
text:
Connecting
find_dyalog checks the command path and standard macOS/Linux installation locations. Pass dyalog= to Apl to choose another executable. timeout bounds the startup handshake, not evaluation.
RIDE uses length-prefixed messages over a local socket. ride_run collects session output until Dyalog is ready for another expression. Interactive and incomplete-input prompts are handled by Apl.run.

title: Dyalog sessions
text:
Evaluating APL
run returns session output as text. Assignments persist across calls:

dyalog = Apl()
out = dyalog.run('x←1 2 3\n+/x')
test_eq(out.strip(), '6')
out

'6\n'


Calling a session returns AplOut, the same text with notebook display support. A silent assignment returns None:

test_is(dyalog('quiet←7'), None)
dyalog('2×x')

2 4 6

title: Dyalog sessions
text:
Python values
pyval uses Dyalog’s JSON conversion. Scalars become Python values and numeric arrays become lists. This is the interface used by the reference checker:

test_eq(dyalog.pyval('+/x'), 6)
matrix = dyalog.pyval('2 3⍴⍳6')
test_eq(matrix, [[1,2,3], [4,5,6]])
matrix

[[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]


Square brackets read an expression or assign a JSON-compatible Python value. Quotes in strings are escaped for APL:

dyalog['values'] = [3,1,4]
dyalog['message'] = "can't"
test_eq(dyalog['message'], "can't")
test_eq(dyalog['values'], [3,1,4])
dyalog['values']

[3, 1, 4]


fn converts Python arguments through JSON and evaluates the function expression on each call. One argument supplies ⍵; two supply ⍺ and ⍵:

mean = dyalog.fn('{(+/⍵)÷≢⍵}')
test_eq(mean([1,2,3]), 2)
add = dyalog.fn('+')
test_eq(add([1,2,3], 10), [11,12,13])
add([1,2,3], 10)

[11, 12, 13]

title: Dyalog sessions
text:
Errors and lifetime
Dyalog errors raise this module’s AplError, not BplError. Completed assignments remain in the session:

with expect_fail(AplError, contains='DOMAIN ERROR'): dyalog.run('saved←42 ⋄ 1÷0')
test_eq(dyalog['saved'], 42)
dyalog['saved']

42


Interactive ⎕ and ⍞ input is rejected. When Dyalog shows an incomplete-input prompt, Apl.run restarts the interpreter and raises AplError with reset=True. The restart loses the workspace.
Call close() when finished, or use a context manager for a bounded reference check:

dyalog.close()
with Apl() as reference: total = reference.pyval('+/⍳10')
test_eq(total, 55)
total

55

text:
Press ▶ Run, or Ctrl-Enter (Cmd-Enter on a Mac), to run the code. Type a backtick and a glyph’s name for a glyph, such as `iota, or click a glyph in the language bar.
The interpreter runs in your browser. It is the latest release of the npm package basedpl. Names you create are persistent between runs. ⏹ Stop ends the session and starts a new one.
